Well, it’s finally happened: Apple has got with the times and finally made a laptop with a touchscreen . However, while the new MacBook Pros with PROLED screens look like fantastic devices, I think Apple has made a mistake by putting its first laptop touchscreen on the more expensive MacBook Pro, rather than the more mainstream MacBook Air… or even the MacBook Neo . The 14-inch MacBook Pro with a touchscreen starts at $2,899 / £2,899 / AU$4,599, and the 16-inch model starts at $3,399 / £3,399 / AU$5,499. That’s a big ask for most people, especially these days. Of course, MacBook Pros, as the name suggests, are aimed at professionals, and thanks to their high-end components, they should really be seen as investments that allow you to speed up your workflow. Interestingly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros come with Apple’s M5 Pro and M5 Max chips . If you want Apple’s latest M6 chip , you’ll need to go for the non-touchscreen 14-inch MacBook Pro that was announced a few days earlier . Perhaps confusingly, the M6 is less powerful than the M5 Pro and M5 Max, and so far there are no hints that Apple is preparing to release M6 Pro and M6 Max chips. My point is that by putting its first-ever laptop touchscreen on its most powerful — and expensive — MacBooks, Apple is severely limiting the potential audience for the technology. Had it instead put a touchscreen on the more affordable MacBook Air, it could have had a real hit on its hands. As someone who has used plenty of Windows laptops and Chromebooks with touchscreens in the past, I know how useful they can be for certain tasks, and I often miss them when using a MacBook. Being able to scroll down a website with a finger, turn a page in an ebook, or quickly tap a menu item feels natural and intuitive, and I’m sure it will on the new MacBooks. My daughter, who grew up with touchscreens on everything, would also instinctively poke an often sticky, grubby (kids, you’ve got to love them!) finger at a MacBook screen and be surprised when nothing happened. If you’re dropping $3,000+ on a touchscreen laptop just to use the touchscreen for browsing websites, then you’re either super-rich or you should get help with your budgeting. These are all pretty simple tasks and gestures. What I've never used touchscreens on laptops for, however, is for complex tasks and tools, such as recording and editing music in Ableton Live, or editing videos in Adobe Premiere Pro. Instead, for things that needed precision or complexity, nothing beat the good old combo of keyboard and touchpad (or even better, keyboard and a mouse), as well as other external peripherals such as MIDI controllers and drawing tablets . Which leads me to wonder why Apple picked the MacBook Pro, a device that’s supposedly designed for exactly those type of tasks, to showcase its first laptop touchscreen. If you’re dropping $3,000+ on a touchscreen laptop to mostly just to use the touchscreen for browsing websites, then you’re either super-rich or you should get help with your budgeting. The 16-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro and no touchscreen starts at $2,999 / £2,999 / AU$4,799. As the MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR touchscreen with the same specs costs $400 / £400 / AU$700 more, that’s quite a premium for the touchscreen. Yes, I know the PROLED XDR screen offers better image quality as well thanks to its tandem OLED tech (check out our explainer on why this is a big deal ), but if you don’t need that additional image quality, which includes better contrast, higher brightness levels, and support for the Adobe RGB color gamut, and are just interested in the touchscreen, then essentially yeah, you’re paying $400 extra for it. If you’re a professional, especially one in the creative industry, you’ll need to think long and hard if that investment is worth it. Meanwhile, the likes of the MacBook Air and MacBook Neo aren’t really used for complex creative tasks, and instead used for casual day-to-day use, where touchscreens are much more useful. Granted, adding an extra $400 / £400 / AU$700 to the price of a MacBook Neo or MacBook Air wouldn’t be great, especially as they’ve just had a price bump earlier this year , but Apple wouldn’t need to include the OLED tech and advanced image-quality options included in the MacBook Pro. A touchscreen MacBook Neo for $899, say, could be a real hit, especially if Apple was to also keep the non-touchscreen model for people who still want the ultimate affordable way to get into the Mac ecosystem. This isn’t just an Apple problem, of course. The new laptops powered by Nvidia’s RTX Spark SoC , which are aimed at the same creative professionals and heavy local AI users as the MacBook Pro (with similarly high price tags), come with touchscreens. I’ve spent a decent amount of time with each one at various events, and I found that the touchscreen was the least-used part of the laptop — in fact, I often forgot those laptops had one. Because there aren’t cheaper, non-touch, models, though I didn’t resent its inclusion. As I said, I do get the appeal of touchscreen laptops, but I find the technology is best used in 2-in-1 devices where the keyboard can be flipped behind the screen (or removed entirely) so that it can be used as a tablet-like device. In an ideal world, then, Apple would have put its touchscreen on an entirely new 2-in-1 MacBook, but I can’t see that happening any time soon. Apple sort of has a device like that — the powerful iPad Pro , which can be paired with a Magic Keyboard that turns it into a touchscreen laptop. The problem there, however, is that despite coming with Apple’s powerful M-series chips, the same you’ll find in MacBooks, the iPad Pro is limited to the iPadOS operating system and mobile apps. Put macOS on that bad boy, however, and allow us to run full desktop applications on it, and hey presto: Apple has a touchscreen MacBook that utilizes the tech in a way that’s actually useful. Until then, I’ll stick with my standard MacBook Pro, and just try to remember not to prod it with my sausage fingers too often. Well, it’s finally happened: Apple has got with the times and finally made a laptop with a touchscreen . However, while the new MacBook Pros with PROLED screens look like fantastic devices, I think Apple has made a mistake by putting its first laptop touchscreen on the more expensive MacBook Pro, rather than the more mainstream MacBook Air… or even the MacBook Neo .
The 14-inch MacBook Pro with a touchscreen starts at $2,899 / £2,899 / AU$4,599, and the 16-inch model starts at $3,399 / £3,399 / AU$5,499. That’s a big ask for most people, especially these days.
Of course, MacBook Pros, as the name suggests, are aimed at professionals, and thanks to their high-end components, they should really be seen as investments that allow you to speed up your workflow.

Interestingly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros come with Apple’s M5 Pro and M5 Max chips . If you want Apple’s latest M6 chip , you’ll need to go for the non-touchscreen 14-inch MacBook Pro that was announced a few days earlier . Perhaps confusingly, the M6 is less powerful than the M5 Pro and M5 Max, and so far there are no hints that Apple is preparing to release M6 Pro and M6 Max chips.

My point is that by putting its first-ever laptop touchscreen on its most powerful — and expensive — MacBooks, Apple is severely limiting the potential audience for the technology. Had it instead put a touchscreen on the more affordable MacBook Air, it could have had a real hit on its hands.
As someone who has used plenty of Windows laptops and Chromebooks with touchscreens in the past, I know how useful they can be for certain tasks, and I often miss them when using a MacBook.

Being able to scroll down a website with a finger, turn a page in an ebook, or quickly tap a menu item feels natural and intuitive, and I’m sure it will on the new MacBooks. My daughter, who grew up with touchscreens on everything, would also instinctively poke an often sticky, grubby (kids, you’ve got to love them!) finger at a MacBook screen and be surprised when nothing happened.
If you’re dropping $3,000+ on a touchscreen laptop just to use the touchscreen for browsing websites, then you’re either super-rich or you should get help with your budgeting.

These are all pretty simple tasks and gestures. What I've never used touchscreens on laptops for, however, is for complex tasks and tools, such as recording and editing music in Ableton Live, or editing videos in Adobe Premiere Pro.

Instead, for things that needed precision or complexity, nothing beat the good old combo of keyboard and touchpad (or even better, keyboard and a mouse), as well as other external peripherals such as MIDI controllers and drawing tablets . Which leads me to wonder why Apple picked the MacBook Pro, a device that’s supposedly designed for exactly those type of tasks, to showcase its first laptop touchscreen.
If you’re dropping $3,000+ on a touchscreen laptop to mostly just to use the touchscreen for browsing websites, then you’re either super-rich or you should get help with your budgeting.

The 16-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro and no touchscreen starts at $2,999 / £2,999 / AU$4,799. As the MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR touchscreen with the same specs costs $400 / £400 / AU$700 more, that’s quite a premium for the touchscreen.

Yes, I know the PROLED XDR screen offers better image quality as well thanks to its tandem OLED tech (check out our explainer on why this is a big deal ), but if you don’t need that additional image quality, which includes better contrast, higher brightness levels, and support for the Adobe RGB color gamut, and are just interested in the touchscreen, then essentially yeah, you’re paying $400 extra for it.

If you’re a professional, especially one in the creative industry, you’ll need to think long and hard if that investment is worth it. Meanwhile, the likes of the MacBook Air and MacBook Neo aren’t really used for complex creative tasks, and instead used for casual day-to-day use, where touchscreens are much more useful.

Granted, adding an extra $400 / £400 / AU$700 to the price of a MacBook Neo or MacBook Air wouldn’t be great, especially as they’ve just had a price bump earlier this year , but Apple wouldn’t need to include the OLED tech and advanced image-quality options included in the MacBook Pro. A touchscreen MacBook Neo for $899, say, could be a real hit, especially if Apple was to also keep the non-touchscreen model for people who still want the ultimate affordable way to get into the Mac ecosystem.

This isn’t just an Apple problem, of course. The new laptops powered by Nvidia’s RTX Spark SoC , which are aimed at the same creative professionals and heavy local AI users as the MacBook Pro (with similarly high price tags), come with touchscreens. I’ve spent a decent amount of time with each one at various events, and I found that the touchscreen was the least-used part of the laptop — in fact, I often forgot those laptops had one. Because there aren’t cheaper, non-touch, models, though I didn’t resent its inclusion.

As I said, I do get the appeal of touchscreen laptops, but I find the technology is best used in 2-in-1 devices where the keyboard can be flipped behind the screen (or removed entirely) so that it can be used as a tablet-like device.

In an ideal world, then, Apple would have put its touchscreen on an entirely new 2-in-1 MacBook, but I can’t see that happening any time soon. Apple sort of has a device like that — the powerful iPad Pro , which can be paired with a Magic Keyboard that turns it into a touchscreen laptop. The problem there, however, is that despite coming with Apple’s powerful M-series chips, the same you’ll find in MacBooks, the iPad Pro is limited to the iPadOS operating system and mobile apps.

Put macOS on that bad boy, however, and allow us to run full desktop applications on it, and hey presto: Apple has a touchscreen MacBook that utilizes the tech in a way that’s actually useful. Until then, I’ll stick with my standard MacBook Pro, and just try to remember not to prod it with my sausage fingers too often.

passages: Apple’s long-awaited touchscreen MacBook Pro is finally here.
This new MacBook Pro looks great as a whole, but there’s more magic in that lid logo than the touchscreen.
When I asked a few of them if they wished the MacBook Pro included Apple Pencil support, nearly all of them said sure, that’d be cool, too.
The hallmark feature — the thing Apple was never going to do until it did — was the touchscreen.
The current Mini LED MacBook Pros are great, but the OLED has those even inkier blacks.
It finally rips off the Band-Aid for Apple and sets the table for touchscreens to one day come to much more attainable laptops, like the MacBook Air and Neo.

extraction.body: Apple’s long-awaited touchscreen MacBook Pro is finally here. I got to try this MacBook that, according to the last two Apple CEOs, shouldn’t exist. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display (what a name) has one of the nicest screens I’ve seen on a laptop. The current Mini LED MacBook Pros are great, but the OLED has those even inkier blacks. It also gets super bright, with incredibly rich colors and infinite contrast. The hallmark feature — the thing Apple was never going to do until it did — was the touchscreen. How would Apple prove that touchscreens on laptops aren’t “ergonomically terrible”? Apple took its time, but it really figured it out”? And it’s just a touchscreen. [Image: We’re just normal touchscreen laptops. It’s cool and all, but it doesn’t exactly look like it’ll reinvent how we use laptops. (Better luck in future macOS updates, I guess?) Over a decade ago, touchscreen laptops were supposed to be revolutionary. Then, Windows 8 crashed and burned, and convertible laptops became just another product segment as opposed to redefining how a laptop looks and works. Apple waited it all out, realized no one cared that much, added a touchscreen with some minor UI improvements, and went, “Okay, enjoy macOS with some swiping.” [Image: This demo from a pro photographer used bracketed exposures and a vibe coded app to composite the images into one interactive photo. It finally rips off the Band-Aid for Apple and sets the table for touchscreens to one day come to much more attainable laptops, like the MacBook Air and Neo. Apple still has lots of touch-based devices for people who want to prioritize that. But this is just normal now: You have a laptop with a keyboard, trackpad, and a touchable screen for whenever you want to poke at it. It’s all very strategic, as is usually the case with Apple. Looking at the touchscreen settings menu, I saw that most touch gestures just map to things you can already do on the trackpad. At Apple’s event, I sat in on briefings that included professionals who recently started using the touchscreen MacBook Pro. When I asked a few of them if they wished the MacBook Pro included Apple Pencil support, nearly all of them said sure, that’d be cool, too. Apple took over a decade to come around to the touchscreen. And bringing back the illuminated Apple logo is just fun! This new MacBook Pro looks great as a whole, but there’s more magic in that lid logo than the touchscreen. Before the event, I wondered how Apple could make a touchscreen laptop better. And, well, it just made a touchscreen laptop.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has suspended withdrawals after hackers stole $6.3 billion U.S. from its platform. The exchange said that a "security incident" had impacted $6.3 billion U.S., in what's being called the worst cryptocurrency attack ever. Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said the exchange will cover all losses from the $6.3 billion U.S. hack and make investors whole again. Cardano Founder Hoskinson Says Midnight Will Surpass Zcash, Urges Gemini to List ADA Stacks Founder Warns Bitcoin Security Breach Could Hit Entire Crypto Market Coinbase Targets Banks As Institutional Crypto Adoption Grows 60 Percent of Community Banks See Stablecoins as a Threat to Deposits, Lending Crypto Heavyweights Back OKX at $25B Valuation However, the crypto exchange has temporarily suspended all withdrawals while it assesses the security breach and the damage done. Binance said an initial investigation suggests "the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access…" Teng said Binance is still assessing the impact to the exchange. He added that there's no evidence of any wallet private keys being stolen. The exchange is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover the stolen funds. Binance also said that deposits to the exchange remain unaffected by the security breach. The company expects to begin resuming withdrawal services within the next 48 hours. Teng also said that Binance is able to cover all losses using its Secure Asset Fund, as well as company funds, adding that customer funds remain safe. Other crypto firms such as Circle Internet Group (NYSE: $CRCL) and Ripple have also temporarily frozen funds that are believed to be tied to the hack. The incident at Binance and size of the theft have rattled confidence in cryptocurrency safety, which many people believe is under threat from artificial intelligence (A.I.) and quantum computers. Bitcoin (CRYPTO: $BTC) fell more than 4% to $77,400 U.S. early on Oct. 30 as news of the hack broke worldwide. Binance is privately held and its stock does not trade on a public exchange.

extraction.body: Binance has confirmed to TechCrunch that it is dealing with a security incident as users reported that funds were being drained from the crypto exchange’s wallets. The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange said in an emailed statement to TechCrunch that it is “aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating.” “Rest assured that user funds are completely safe,” Binance said in a statement. “Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information,” the statement added. “Users should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.” Binance spokesperson Ross O’Leary said that Binance has “temporarily suspended withdrawals on multiple networks following a security incident as a precautionary measure.” News of the breach comes hours after Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said in a post on X that the company likely had been hacked. Zhao, who no longer runs the company but is its largest shareholder, said that he expects users’ funds to be “fully covered” but did not provide an explanation for the claim. Financial tech giant Circle froze about $800 million in Tether as it passed through its networks, while crypto giant Tether froze about $1.56 billion related to Binance’s hack. Crypto watchers say at least $2 billion has been drained from Binance’s hot wallets, which are internet-connected cryptocurrency wallets that store crypto that are connected to the internet. By some estimates, Binance may have lost upward of $5.7 billion in crypto , though the numbers have not been confirmed and it’s possible that the theft is ongoing. It’s unclear who is behind the hack, and Binance did not say if it had received any correspondence from the hackers. If confirmed into the billions, this would likely rank as one of the largest crypto breaches in history, according to leaderboards tracking crypto thefts. In 2025, hackers stole a record $1.4 billion in crypto in a single breach from exchange Bybit, blamed on North Korean hackers. In what appears to be a separate incident earlier on Thursday, prediction market giant Polymarket briefly halted trading after it confirmed that a third-party company was compromised, which led to the company pausing withdrawals. According to security researchers, hackers stole around $2 million in user funds after compromising a piece of software developed by a company called DebugBear . sources.title: Hackers steal $6.3 billion from Binance in record heist blamed on North Korea
passages: Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a record theft that analysts pinned on North Korea and said could shake faith in digital assets.
“This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it,” Binance said in a ​post on X.
Cryptocurrency prices fell on the news, while Binance halted withdrawals and said it would cover the losses.
About half the stolen assets were quickly frozen by stablecoin issuers such as Tether, Circle and the Trump-backed World Liberty Financial.

sources.title: Binance Rocked by $6.3B Crypto Heist as Hackers Drain Wallets and Exchange Freezes Withdrawals
passages: About $6.36 billion (£4.75 billion) was transferred out of Binance wallets in minutes in what analysts say is among the biggest cryptocurrency thefts on record, prompting other major crypto firms to freeze billions of dollars linked to the incident.The attack took place on 29 October, with blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs tracking transfers from Binance wallets across ten blockchains.

The exact method used by the attacker remains under investigation.TRM Labs gave a detailed account of the Ethereum transactions, saying the attacker exploited an EIP-7702 delegation feature to turn a Binance hot wallet into a mechanism that automatically forwarded incoming funds to an attacker-controlled address.Transfers from wallets on the other nine blockchains involved ordinary signed transactions, according to the firm.Binance co-CEO Richard Teng has said customer funds are safe and that the exchange will cover the losses.
The exchange said it had found no evidence of a wallet private-key leak.Binance later said its investigation had uncovered additional points of breach, without publicly detailing them.

Tether and Circle can restrict transactions involving their own stablecoins, but they cannot freeze Bitcoin or Ether held in a private wallet.Stablecoins such as USDT and USDC are issued and managed by companies that can intervene in transactions involving their tokens.

Bitcoin and Ethereum operate on public blockchains without a central issuer that can block or reverse movements of funds in the same way.Binance Security Under ScrutinyBinance's initial investigation suggested that a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop may have allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions.

The company said it would use its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, and its own resources to meet the shortfall.The Block reported that Binance had allocated more than $6.34 billion in company funds and reserves for that purpose, including approximately $5 billion (£3.7 billion) in affected digital assets, with the remainder being acquired.

Most of the money was moved in about 20 minutes. Binance estimated the impact at around $6.3 billion, while TRM put the figure at $6.36 billion.Following the incident, other large cryptocurrency firms moved to block assets connected to the suspected theft.Billions Frozen, but the Money Is Still MissingTRM Labs said Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial froze approximately $2.67 billion (£1.99 billion) in stablecoins linked to the incident. Arbitrum's Security Council separately froze 8,426 ETH and 74.6 million ARB, bringing the total frozen to roughly $2.7 billion.Tether chief executive Paolo Ardoino said the company had frozen more than $1.57 billion (£1.1 billion) in USDT. Circle, the issuer of USDC, froze more than $800 million (£6 million), according to reporting by The Block and CoinDesk. Ripple and World Liberty Financial also participated in the response.World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency venture associated with the Trump family, was reported to have frozen approximately $27 million (£20 million) in its USD1 stablecoin.The frozen assets have not been automatically returned to Binance or its customers. Billions in other cryptocurrencies linked to the incident remain outside the direct control of those companies.The Coins Even Crypto Giants Cannot TouchTRM Labs estimated that the attacker still held more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth approximately $2.4 billion (£1.79 billion) at the time of its assessment.Unlike USDT and USDC, Bitcoin and Ethereum are not issued by a central company with the power to blacklist individual tokens. Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has suspended withdrawals after hackers stole $6.3 billion U.S. from its platform. The exchange said that a "security incident" had impacted $6.3 billion U.S., in what's being called the worst cryptocurrency attack ever. Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said the exchange will cover all losses from the $6.3 billion U.S. hack and make investors whole again. Cardano Founder Hoskinson Says Midnight Will Surpass Zcash, Urges Gemini to List ADA Stacks Founder Warns Bitcoin Security Breach Could Hit Entire Crypto Market Coinbase Targets Banks As Institutional Crypto Adoption Grows 60 Percent of Community Banks See Stablecoins as a Threat to Deposits, Lending Crypto Heavyweights Back OKX at $25B Valuation However, the crypto exchange has temporarily suspended all withdrawals while it assesses the security breach and the damage done. Binance said an initial investigation suggests "the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access…" Teng said Binance is still assessing the impact to the exchange. He added that there's no evidence of any wallet private keys being stolen. The exchange is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover the stolen funds. Binance also said that deposits to the exchange remain unaffected by the security breach. The company expects to begin resuming withdrawal services within the next 48 hours. Teng also said that Binance is able to cover all losses using its Secure Asset Fund, as well as company funds, adding that customer funds remain safe. Other crypto firms such as Circle Internet Group (NYSE: $CRCL) and Ripple have also temporarily frozen funds that are believed to be tied to the hack. The incident at Binance and size of the theft have rattled confidence in cryptocurrency safety, which many people believe is under threat from artificial intelligence (A.I.) and quantum computers. Bitcoin (CRYPTO: $BTC) fell more than 4% to $77,400 U.S. early on Oct. 30 as news of the hack broke worldwide. Binance is privately held and its stock does not trade on a public exchange.

extraction.body: Binance has confirmed to TechCrunch that it is dealing with a security incident as users reported that funds were being drained from the crypto exchange’s wallets. The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange said in an emailed statement to TechCrunch that it is “aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating.” “Rest assured that user funds are completely safe,” Binance said in a statement. “Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information,” the statement added. “Users should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.” Binance spokesperson Ross O’Leary said that Binance has “temporarily suspended withdrawals on multiple networks following a security incident as a precautionary measure.” News of the breach comes hours after Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said in a post on X that the company likely had been hacked. Zhao, who no longer runs the company but is its largest shareholder, said that he expects users’ funds to be “fully covered” but did not provide an explanation for the claim. Financial tech giant Circle froze about $800 million in Tether as it passed through its networks, while crypto giant Tether froze about $1.56 billion related to Binance’s hack. Crypto watchers say at least $2 billion has been drained from Binance’s hot wallets, which are internet-connected cryptocurrency wallets that store crypto that are connected to the internet. By some estimates, Binance may have lost upward of $5.7 billion in crypto , though the numbers have not been confirmed and it’s possible that the theft is ongoing. It’s unclear who is behind the hack, and Binance did not say if it had received any correspondence from the hackers. If confirmed into the billions, this would likely rank as one of the largest crypto breaches in history, according to leaderboards tracking crypto thefts. In 2025, hackers stole a record $1.4 billion in crypto in a single breach from exchange Bybit, blamed on North Korean hackers. In what appears to be a separate incident earlier on Thursday, prediction market giant Polymarket briefly halted trading after it confirmed that a third-party company was compromised, which led to the company pausing withdrawals. According to security researchers, hackers stole around $2 million in user funds after compromising a piece of software developed by a company called DebugBear . sources.title: Hackers steal $6.3 billion from Binance in record heist blamed on North Korea
passages: Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a record theft that analysts pinned on North Korea and said could shake faith in digital assets.
“This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it,” Binance said in a ​post on X.
Cryptocurrency prices fell on the news, while Binance halted withdrawals and said it would cover the losses.
About half the stolen assets were quickly frozen by stablecoin issuers such as Tether, Circle and the Trump-backed World Liberty Financial.

sources.title: Binance Rocked by $6.3B Crypto Heist as Hackers Drain Wallets and Exchange Freezes Withdrawals
passages: About $6.36 billion (£4.75 billion) was transferred out of Binance wallets in minutes in what analysts say is among the biggest cryptocurrency thefts on record, prompting other major crypto firms to freeze billions of dollars linked to the incident.The attack took place on 29 October, with blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs tracking transfers from Binance wallets across ten blockchains.

The exact method used by the attacker remains under investigation.TRM Labs gave a detailed account of the Ethereum transactions, saying the attacker exploited an EIP-7702 delegation feature to turn a Binance hot wallet into a mechanism that automatically forwarded incoming funds to an attacker-controlled address.Transfers from wallets on the other nine blockchains involved ordinary signed transactions, according to the firm.Binance co-CEO Richard Teng has said customer funds are safe and that the exchange will cover the losses.
The exchange said it had found no evidence of a wallet private-key leak.Binance later said its investigation had uncovered additional points of breach, without publicly detailing them.

Tether and Circle can restrict transactions involving their own stablecoins, but they cannot freeze Bitcoin or Ether held in a private wallet.Stablecoins such as USDT and USDC are issued and managed by companies that can intervene in transactions involving their tokens.

Bitcoin and Ethereum operate on public blockchains without a central issuer that can block or reverse movements of funds in the same way.Binance Security Under ScrutinyBinance's initial investigation suggested that a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop may have allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions.

The company said it would use its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, and its own resources to meet the shortfall.The Block reported that Binance had allocated more than $6.34 billion in company funds and reserves for that purpose, including approximately $5 billion (£3.7 billion) in affected digital assets, with the remainder being acquired.

extraction.body: About $6.36 billion (£4.75 billion) was transferred out of Binance wallets in minutes in what analysts say is among the biggest cryptocurrency thefts on record, prompting other major crypto firms to freeze billions of dollars linked to the incident.The attack took place on 29 October, with blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs tracking transfers from Binance wallets across ten blockchains. Most of the money was moved in about 20 minutes. Binance estimated the impact at around $6.3 billion, while TRM put the figure at $6.36 billion.Following the incident, other large cryptocurrency firms moved to block assets connected to the suspected theft.Billions Frozen, but the Money Is Still MissingTRM Labs said Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial froze approximately $2.67 billion (£1.99 billion) in stablecoins linked to the incident. Arbitrum's Security Council separately froze 8,426 ETH and 74.6 million ARB, bringing the total frozen to roughly $2.7 billion.Tether chief executive Paolo Ardoino said the company had frozen more than $1.57 billion (£1.1 billion) in USDT. Circle, the issuer of USDC, froze more than $800 million (£6 million), according to reporting by The Block and CoinDesk. Ripple and World Liberty Financial also participated in the response.World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency venture associated with the Trump family, was reported to have frozen approximately $27 million (£20 million) in its USD1 stablecoin.The frozen assets have not been automatically returned to Binance or its customers. Billions in other cryptocurrencies linked to the incident remain outside the direct control of those companies.The Coins Even Crypto Giants Cannot TouchTRM Labs estimated that the attacker still held more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth approximately $2.4 billion (£1.79 billion) at the time of its assessment.Unlike USDT and USDC, Bitcoin and Ethereum are not issued by a central company with the power to blacklist individual tokens. Tether and Circle can restrict transactions involving their own stablecoins, but they cannot freeze Bitcoin or Ether held in a private wallet.Stablecoins such as USDT and USDC are issued and managed by companies that can intervene in transactions involving their tokens. Bitcoin and Ethereum operate on public blockchains without a central issuer that can block or reverse movements of funds in the same way.Binance Security Under ScrutinyBinance's initial investigation suggested that a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop may have allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions. The exchange said it had found no evidence of a wallet private-key leak.Binance later said its investigation had uncovered additional points of breach, without publicly detailing them. The exact method used by the attacker remains under investigation.TRM Labs gave a detailed account of the Ethereum transactions, saying the attacker exploited an EIP-7702 delegation feature to turn a Binance hot wallet into a mechanism that automatically forwarded incoming funds to an attacker-controlled address.Transfers from wallets on the other nine blockchains involved ordinary signed transactions, according to the firm.Binance co-CEO Richard Teng has said customer funds are safe and that the exchange will cover the losses. The company said it would use its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, and its own resources to meet the shortfall.The Block reported that Binance had allocated more than $6.34 billion in company funds and reserves for that purpose, including approximately $5 billion (£3.7 billion) in affected digital assets, with the remainder being acquired. That commitment is separate from the approximately $3 billion (£2.2 billion) frozen by industry partners.North Korean Link Probed, but Not ProvenTRM Labs has attributed the attack with 'high confidence' to TraderTraitor, a hacking unit it says is linked to North Korea. Reuters reported the firm's assessment, and other blockchain investigators have also pointed to possible North Korean involvement.Binance has not publicly confirmed this attribution. The company has said it is working with law enforcement and intelligence partners to identify those responsible.TRM Labs compared the theft with the February 2025 Bybit attack, in which approximately $1.5 billion (£1.1 billion) was stolen.The Binance incident involved what TRM Labs and Binance estimate to be more than $6.3 billion in unauthorised withdrawals, making it one of the largest reported cryptocurrency thefts to date.

extraction.body: General Motors on Thursday agreed to pay $220 million to settle a lawsuit filed by a coalition of 36 state attorneys general who alleged the company unlawfully sold consumers’ location and driving behavior data to outside parties, including data brokers. The data brokers then sold the sensitive data to insurers, affecting the prices drivers were charged for insurance, according to a press release from Washington Attorney General Nick Brown, who co-led the coalition’s efforts. In addition to the fine, the settlement requires GM to ask customers for their affirmative express consent prior to collecting or sharing consumer driving behavior and location data Beginning in 2016 and running through 2024, when the New York Times exposed the practice, GM allegedly enrolled millions of people in their “Smart Driver” program, allowing the auto giant to monitor their driving habits. The company allegedly marketed the program to customers by emphasizing participation could help drivers bolster their driving safety. The manufacturer also allegedly promised customers that it would not give insurers their data without their affirmative consent. However, GM allegedly broke that promise by selling the information to data brokers despite contract language it signed indicating the brokers planned to profit by providing the data to insurers. GM did not tell participating customers they would do so, the suit alleged. A GM spokesperson said in an emailed statement that the “agreement addresses Smart Driver, a product we ended in 2024, and reinforces steps we’ve taken to strengthen our privacy practices.” “Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share,” they said. Most customers agreed to participate in the Smart Driver program at dealerships as they were purchasing cars, and many have described pressure tactics that convinced them to sign. The one time sign-up process for drivers to enroll in Smart Driver also swept them into GM’s OnStar services. The data collection system operated with built-in factory surveillance far exceeding what insurers could collect by offering customers discounts to sign up for their own driving behavior trackers. Dealership employees were allegedly given bonuses for successfully enrolling customers in Smart Driver and dealerships also received incentives with GM ranking them against each other based on enrollment numbers, the press release said. The automaker also mistakenly informed more than 370,000 customers their data was not being monitored because they were not enrolled in Smart Driver, the attorneys general contend. GM subsequently unenrolled the drivers, but allegedly did so secretly and without alerting customers to the mistake. The data that had already been collected was allegedly not withdrawn from the data brokers and insurers. “The data GM sold was personal, identifiable, and specific,” the press release said. “Insurers had data showing how many times a person drove their vehicle, the start and end times of each drive, how many times they braked or accelerated quickly, and whether they went faster than the speed limit.” Following an outcry prompted by the New York Times’ revelations, GM shut down the program. Under the settlement, GM must minimize the driving data it takes from consumers and safeguard their information as part of a comprehensive data privacy program, the press release said. The settlement terms are “significantly stronger than any other resolution reached with GM for this conduct including by mandating internal and external data protection and privacy program assessments,” the press release said. GM also agreed to augment oversight and training for dealership employees to ensure they do not sign customers up for data collection programs without their approval. A similar lawsuit filed against GM by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in 2024 is ongoing. Paxton has alleged the car manufacturer handled drivers’ data in a “false, deceptive, and misleading” way by collecting data from customers, selling it to data brokers and allowing the brokers to in turn peddle it to insurers. Texas is seeking a jury trial and civil penalties of up to $10,000 per offense, along with a court order directing GM to delete the collected data. is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children. © Copyright 2026 | The Record from Recorded Future News

The data brokers then sold the sensitive data to insurers, affecting the prices drivers were charged for insurance, according to a press release from Washington Attorney General Nick Brown, who co-led the coalition’s efforts.
In addition to the fine, the settlement requires GM to ask customers for their affirmative express consent prior to collecting or sharing consumer driving behavior and location data

Beginning in 2016 and running through 2024, when the New York Times exposed the practice, GM allegedly enrolled millions of people in their “Smart Driver” program, allowing the auto giant to monitor their driving habits.

The company allegedly marketed the program to customers by emphasizing participation could help drivers bolster their driving safety. The manufacturer also allegedly promised customers that it would not give insurers their data without their affirmative consent.

However, GM allegedly broke that promise by selling the information to data brokers despite contract language it signed indicating the brokers planned to profit by providing the data to insurers. GM did not tell participating customers they would do so, the suit alleged.
A GM spokesperson said in an emailed statement that the “agreement addresses Smart Driver, a product we ended in 2024, and reinforces steps we’ve taken to strengthen our privacy practices.”

“Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share,” they said.
Most customers agreed to participate in the Smart Driver program at dealerships as they were purchasing cars, and many have described pressure tactics that convinced them to sign.

The one time sign-up process for drivers to enroll in Smart Driver also swept them into GM’s OnStar services. The data collection system operated with built-in factory surveillance far exceeding what insurers could collect by offering customers discounts to sign up for their own driving behavior trackers.

Dealership employees were allegedly given bonuses for successfully enrolling customers in Smart Driver and dealerships also received incentives with GM ranking them against each other based on enrollment numbers, the press release said.

The automaker also mistakenly informed more than 370,000 customers their data was not being monitored because they were not enrolled in Smart Driver, the attorneys general contend. GM subsequently unenrolled the drivers, but allegedly did so secretly and without alerting customers to the mistake. The data that had already been collected was allegedly not withdrawn from the data brokers and insurers.

“The data GM sold was personal, identifiable, and specific,” the press release said. “Insurers had data showing how many times a person drove their vehicle, the start and end times of each drive, how many times they braked or accelerated quickly, and whether they went faster than the speed limit.”
Following an outcry prompted by the New York Times’ revelations, GM shut down the program.
Under the settlement, GM must minimize the driving data it takes from consumers and safeguard their information as part of a comprehensive data privacy program, the press release said.

The settlement terms are “significantly stronger than any other resolution reached with GM for this conduct including by mandating internal and external data protection and privacy program assessments,” the press release said.
GM also agreed to augment oversight and training for dealership employees to ensure they do not sign customers up for data collection programs without their approval.
A similar lawsuit filed against GM by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in 2024 is ongoing.

Paxton has alleged the car manufacturer handled drivers’ data in a “false, deceptive, and misleading” way by collecting data from customers, selling it to data brokers and allowing the brokers to in turn peddle it to insurers.
Texas is seeking a jury trial and civil penalties of up to $10,000 per offense, along with a court order directing GM to delete the collected data.

is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

The Federal Trade Commission announced a proposed settlement with the company in January 2025 and finalized it in January 2026, banning GM from disclosing certain driver location and behavior data to consumer reporting agencies for five years.
California followed in May 2026 with a separate $12.75 million settlement after authorities alleged that GM sold data belonging to hundreds of thousands of Californians.
The multistate complaint says GM made more than $20 million from data sales nationwide, while California law barred insurers from using driving behavior to set rates.
Stack the federal consent order, the California deal and this week's 36-state settlement together: GM has now been fined, banned and re-regulated three separate times for the same underlying conduct.

According to the attorneys general, they were also largely hidden from the people whose data was being collected. GM's OnStar system logged how hard customers braked, how fast they drove and when they were on the road, then packaged that behavioral data and sold it to Verisk Analytics and LexisNexis Risk Solutions. Those firms, in turn, sold it to insurance companies, who used it to help set premiums. A driver who never got a ticket could still see their rate climb: an algorithm somewhere had decided their 11 p.m. commute looked risky. The data brokers then sold the sensitive data to insurers, affecting the prices drivers were charged for insurance, according to a press release from Washington Attorney General Nick Brown, who co-led the coalition’s efforts. In addition to the fine, the settlement requires GM to ask customers for their affirmative express consent prior to collecting or sharing consumer driving behavior and location data Beginning in 2016 and running through 2024, when the New York Times exposed the practice, GM allegedly enrolled millions of people in their “Smart Driver” program, allowing the auto giant to monitor their driving habits. The company allegedly marketed the program to customers by emphasizing participation could help drivers bolster their driving safety. The manufacturer also allegedly promised customers that it would not give insurers their data without their affirmative consent. However, GM allegedly broke that promise by selling the information to data brokers despite contract language it signed indicating the brokers planned to profit by providing the data to insurers. GM did not tell participating customers they would do so, the suit alleged. A GM spokesperson said in an emailed statement that the “agreement addresses Smart Driver, a product we ended in 2024, and reinforces steps we’ve taken to strengthen our privacy practices.” “Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share,” they said. Most customers agreed to participate in the Smart Driver program at dealerships as they were purchasing cars, and many have described pressure tactics that convinced them to sign. The one time sign-up process for drivers to enroll in Smart Driver also swept them into GM’s OnStar services. A GM spokesperson said in an emailed statement that the “agreement addresses Smart Driver, a product we ended in 2024, and reinforces steps we’ve taken to strengthen our privacy practices.”

“Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share,” they said.
Most customers agreed to participate in the Smart Driver program at dealerships as they were purchasing cars, and many have described pressure tactics that convinced them to sign.

The one time sign-up process for drivers to enroll in Smart Driver also swept them into GM’s OnStar services. Massachusetts alone will receive $5.7 million of the total.

Connected-car features sold to consumers as safety or convenience tools turned out to double as data pipelines feeding the insurance industry, sometimes for only a few cents per vehicle.

sources.title: Waymo’s newest robotaxi is Chinese-made, built to make money, and now accepting riders - TechCrunch
passages: Waymo has started giving select riders in Los Angeles, Phoenix, and San Francisco access to its newest robotaxi: an all-electric, minivan-like vehicle that is designed to lower costs and handle the use and abuse of hundreds of thousands of riders.
The companies partnered in 2021 and showed off a concept of the purpose-built robotaxi in late 2022.
Waymo has spent nearly two years testing the prototype, and later a production-intent version of the vehicle on public roads.
The stripped-down Zeekr vehicles — which don’t contain any Chinese connected car tech — are sent to Waymo’s Arizona factory, where they are outfitted with all of its robotaxi bells and whistles.
Waymo said Thursday it will eventually expand access to the vehicle, a modified Zeekr-made minivan called the Ojai (pronounced oh-hi), to more riders and cities.
For now, the Alphabet-owned company is offering a limited number of customers free rides in the Ojai to gather feedback and further refine the robotaxi experience.
The Ojai is supposed to reflect the technological progress and lessons the company has learned from giving more than 500,000 paid robotaxi rides every week.
This means it can be applied to multiple kinds of vehicles, including two that have already been announced, the Zeekr minivan and the Hyundai Ioniq 5.
Waymo also paused services in Atlanta, Georgia and San Antonio, Texas to address problems with flooding in those cities .

extraction.body: Waymo has started giving select riders in Los Angeles, Phoenix, and San Francisco access to its newest robotaxi: an all-electric, minivan-like vehicle that is designed to lower costs and handle the use and abuse of hundreds of thousands of riders. Waymo said Thursday it will eventually expand access to the vehicle, a modified Zeekr-made minivan called the Ojai (pronounced oh-hi), to more riders and cities. For now, the Alphabet-owned company is offering a limited number of customers free rides in the Ojai to gather feedback and further refine the robotaxi experience. The launch of the Ojai comes after years of development and testing — all in the pursuit of creating a vehicle that is accessible, comfortable, easy-to-maintain, and that importantly costs less to build and operate. Its arrival also comes amid a challenging time for Waymo, which recently suspended robotaxi service on freeways in Los Angeles, Miami, Phoenix, and San Francisco to improve how its vehicles behave in construction zones. Waymo also paused services in Atlanta, Georgia and San Antonio, Texas to address problems with flooding in those cities . The launch of the blue-hued minivan might not wipe the slate clean for Waymo, but it does give the company a real chance at scale and revenue generation. While the vehicle is loaded with Waymo’s hardware and software, its foundation comes from Zeekr, the brand owned by China’s Geely Holding Group. The companies partnered in 2021 and showed off a concept of the purpose-built robotaxi in late 2022. Waymo has spent nearly two years testing the prototype, and later a production-intent version of the vehicle on public roads. The minivan, which was designed in Sweden and manufactured in China, is based on the SEA-M architecture, a refined version of Zeekr’s original Sustainable Experience Architecture (SEA) meant for “future mobility products” like robotaxis and logistics vehicles. The Ojai is equipped with Waymo’s sixth-generation system — including 13 cameras, four lidar sensors, six radar units, and an array of external audio receivers. That sixth-generation system is the keystone to Waymo’s commercial strategy because it’s designed to be modular. This means it can be applied to multiple kinds of vehicles, including two that have already been announced, the Zeekr minivan and the Hyundai Ioniq 5. The Ojai is supposed to reflect the technological progress and lessons the company has learned from giving more than 500,000 paid robotaxi rides every week. And it’s also meant to accelerate the growth of Waymo’s fleet, which today is about 3,700 Jaguar I-Pace vehicles. The stripped-down Zeekr vehicles — which don’t contain any Chinese connected car tech — are sent to Waymo’s Arizona factory, where they are outfitted with all of its robotaxi bells and whistles. The company said it is now scaling toward a capacity of tens of thousands of units annually starting with the Ojai, and followed by the Hyundai Ioniq 5. The result is a vehicle with a flat floor, low step-in height, and gondola-like doors on both sides for easier entry and exit. There are other features aimed at pleasing riders, including charging ports, cup holders, increased leg and head room, grab bars, braille above various buttons, and three large adaptive screens, where customers can access the route, change music, control climate, and provide rider tips. It also has an easier-to-clean interior, faster charging, a modular design, and increased battery capacity — all details that can help reduce costs and make maintenance and repairs more efficient. sources.title: Waymo’s next robotaxi is a purpose-built Toyota bZ4X
passages: Waymo announced today that it will use Toyota bZ4X electric vehicles that are assembled in Japan for a robotaxi service in Tokyo.

And the company is working with Woven by Toyota, the automaker’s software and mobility spinout, to use Waymo’s operational and safety telemetry to improve road safety across general vehicle fleets and traffic infrastructure.
The news builds on the strategic partnership between Waymo and Toyota which was first announced in April 2025.

The decision to build the sensor suite and compute into the bZ4X on Toyota’s own assembly line could help eliminate redundant labor, bespoke brackets, and secondary shipping — and possibly bring down costs for Waymo.
Waymo also says it is continuing to explore integrating its technology into Toyota vehicles for personally owned autonomous vehicles.
The robotaxis will be built entirely under one roof at Toyota’s Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, Japan.
Instead of building regular cars and modifying them later, the factory will install Waymo’s self-driving sensors and computers right on the assembly line as each car is made.
Currently, Waymo uses two vehicle models on the road today — the Jaguar I-Pace and Ojai based on the Zeekr RT — with a third based on the Hyundai Ioniq 5 set to deploy soon.
By adding the bZ4X, Waymo is attempting to prove that its autonomous driving technology is compatible with a wide range of vehicle types.
Waymo has long positioned itself as a software and systems supplier — the “Waymo Driver” — rather than an automaker.
This also represents a shift in terms of how Waymo acquires and modifies the vehicles that end up in its fleet.

sources.title: Waymo picks Toyota bZ4X as its next robotaxi, starting in Japan in 2027 - Electrek
passages: Waymo is adding the Toyota bZ4X to its robotaxi lineup.
Toyota will build a custom version of the electric SUV with the Waymo Driver integrated right on the line in Japan, and a test fleet will start operating there in 2027.
The UK and “other Waymo markets” come in later years, with no dates attached.
The timing lines up with Waymo’s Japan plans.

In September, Waymo said it’s targeting fully driverless commercial rides in Tokyo in 2027 with taxi operator Nihon Kotsu and ride-hailing app GO, scaling to about 100 vehicles, pending regulatory approval.
Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov said that “Toyota’s commitment to zero traffic accidents resonates deeply with us at Waymo.”
Yes, the bZ4X had a rough start (Toyota recalled the first batch in 2022 because the wheels could come off).
But it has come a long way now – becoming boring and reliable.

According to Waymo’s announcement , Toyota will produce the vehicles at its Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, and Waymo’s self-driving hardware will be installed and integrated at that same site instead of being retrofitted somewhere else.
It isn’t Toyota’s first robotaxi bZ4X either: Toyota and Pony.ai started mass-producing bZ4X-based robotaxis in China earlier this year.
In the US, Waymo’s fleet is still mostly made up of Jaguar I-Pace SUVs, a model Jaguar no longer produces.
It’s been adding the Zeekr-built Ojai van and the Hyundai Ioniq 5, and Hyundai is reportedly in talks to supply up to 50,000 Ioniq 5 robotaxis by 2028 .
Waymo’s biggest constraint right now is cars.
It has been running a fleet built on a discontinued Jaguar, and every new automaker it signs adds manufacturing capacity it doesn’t have to build itself.
Toyota is the world’s best-selling automaker.
Having it build Waymo-ready vehicles on its own assembly line is exactly the kind of industrial partner Waymo needed.
I believe it is simply a matter of time before it happens.
But what interests me most is the personal-vehicle angle.
Toyota and Waymo keep mentioning it, but there’s still nothing concrete.
Will that happen before the end of the decade?
When Waymo and Toyota first announced their deal in April 2025 , it was a preliminary agreement to “explore” working together on autonomous driving, including in personally owned vehicles.
The robotaxi bZ4X gets a few rider-focused changes: extra rear legroom, automatic doors, a power liftgate, and ambient lighting.
Waymo didn’t share sensor specs, unit volumes, or what each vehicle costs.
For US readers, the refreshed model is sold here simply as the Toyota bZ, starting at $34,900.
A cheap, high-volume base vehicle matters a lot when you’re trying to scale a fleet.
It’s the first actual vehicle to come out of the partnership the two companies signed last year.
Waymo keeps plugging its driver into existing EVs from established automakers and expanding city by city.

coreStoryFacts.text: Waymo has started giving select riders in Los Angeles, Phoenix, and San Francisco access to its newest robotaxi: an all-electric, minivan-like vehicle that is designed to lower costs and handle the use and abuse of hundreds of thousands of riders.
The companies partnered in 2021 and showed off a concept of the purpose-built robotaxi in late 2022.
Waymo has spent nearly two years testing the prototype, and later a production-intent version of the vehicle on public roads.
The stripped-down Zeekr vehicles — which don’t contain any Chinese connected car tech — are sent to Waymo’s Arizona factory, where they are outfitted with all of its robotaxi bells and whistles.
Waymo said Thursday it will eventually expand access to the vehicle, a modified Zeekr-made minivan called the Ojai (pronounced oh-hi), to more riders and cities.
For now, the Alphabet-owned company is offering a limited number of customers free rides in the Ojai to gather feedback and further refine the robotaxi experience.
The Ojai is supposed to reflect the technological progress and lessons the company has learned from giving more than 500,000 paid robotaxi rides every week.
This means it can be applied to multiple kinds of vehicles, including two that have already been announced, the Zeekr minivan and the Hyundai Ioniq 5.
Waymo also paused services in Atlanta, Georgia and San Antonio, Texas to address problems with flooding in those cities .

The launch of the blue-hued minivan might not wipe the slate clean for Waymo, but it does give the company a real chance at scale and revenue generation.
Waymo announced today that it will use Toyota bZ4X electric vehicles that are assembled in Japan for a robotaxi service in Tokyo.

And the company is working with Woven by Toyota, the automaker’s software and mobility spinout, to use Waymo’s operational and safety telemetry to improve road safety across general vehicle fleets and traffic infrastructure.
The news builds on the strategic partnership between Waymo and Toyota which was first announced in April 2025.

The decision to build the sensor suite and compute into the bZ4X on Toyota’s own assembly line could help eliminate redundant labor, bespoke brackets, and secondary shipping — and possibly bring down costs for Waymo.
Waymo also says it is continuing to explore integrating its technology into Toyota vehicles for personally owned autonomous vehicles.
The robotaxis will be built entirely under one roof at Toyota’s Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, Japan.
Instead of building regular cars and modifying them later, the factory will install Waymo’s self-driving sensors and computers right on the assembly line as each car is made.
Currently, Waymo uses two vehicle models on the road today — the Jaguar I-Pace and Ojai based on the Zeekr RT — with a third based on the Hyundai Ioniq 5 set to deploy soon.
By adding the bZ4X, Waymo is attempting to prove that its autonomous driving technology is compatible with a wide range of vehicle types.
Waymo has long positioned itself as a software and systems supplier — the “Waymo Driver” — rather than an automaker.
This also represents a shift in terms of how Waymo acquires and modifies the vehicles that end up in its fleet.

extraction.body: Waymo has started giving select riders in Los Angeles, Phoenix, and San Francisco access to its newest robotaxi: an all-electric, minivan-like vehicle that is designed to lower costs and handle the use and abuse of hundreds of thousands of riders. Waymo said Thursday it will eventually expand access to the vehicle, a modified Zeekr-made minivan called the Ojai (pronounced oh-hi), to more riders and cities. For now, the Alphabet-owned company is offering a limited number of customers free rides in the Ojai to gather feedback and further refine the robotaxi experience. The launch of the Ojai comes after years of development and testing — all in the pursuit of creating a vehicle that is accessible, comfortable, easy-to-maintain, and that importantly costs less to build and operate. Its arrival also comes amid a challenging time for Waymo, which recently suspended robotaxi service on freeways in Los Angeles, Miami, Phoenix, and San Francisco to improve how its vehicles behave in construction zones. Waymo also paused services in Atlanta, Georgia and San Antonio, Texas to address problems with flooding in those cities . The launch of the blue-hued minivan might not wipe the slate clean for Waymo, but it does give the company a real chance at scale and revenue generation. While the vehicle is loaded with Waymo’s hardware and software, its foundation comes from Zeekr, the brand owned by China’s Geely Holding Group. The companies partnered in 2021 and showed off a concept of the purpose-built robotaxi in late 2022. Waymo has spent nearly two years testing the prototype, and later a production-intent version of the vehicle on public roads. The minivan, which was designed in Sweden and manufactured in China, is based on the SEA-M architecture, a refined version of Zeekr’s original Sustainable Experience Architecture (SEA) meant for “future mobility products” like robotaxis and logistics vehicles. The Ojai is equipped with Waymo’s sixth-generation system — including 13 cameras, four lidar sensors, six radar units, and an array of external audio receivers. That sixth-generation system is the keystone to Waymo’s commercial strategy because it’s designed to be modular. This means it can be applied to multiple kinds of vehicles, including two that have already been announced, the Zeekr minivan and the Hyundai Ioniq 5. The Ojai is supposed to reflect the technological progress and lessons the company has learned from giving more than 500,000 paid robotaxi rides every week. And it’s also meant to accelerate the growth of Waymo’s fleet, which today is about 3,700 Jaguar I-Pace vehicles. The stripped-down Zeekr vehicles — which don’t contain any Chinese connected car tech — are sent to Waymo’s Arizona factory, where they are outfitted with all of its robotaxi bells and whistles. The company said it is now scaling toward a capacity of tens of thousands of units annually starting with the Ojai, and followed by the Hyundai Ioniq 5. The result is a vehicle with a flat floor, low step-in height, and gondola-like doors on both sides for easier entry and exit. There are other features aimed at pleasing riders, including charging ports, cup holders, increased leg and head room, grab bars, braille above various buttons, and three large adaptive screens, where customers can access the route, change music, control climate, and provide rider tips. It also has an easier-to-clean interior, faster charging, a modular design, and increased battery capacity — all details that can help reduce costs and make maintenance and repairs more efficient. The launch of the Ojai comes after years of development and testing — all in the pursuit of creating a vehicle that is accessible, comfortable, easy-to-maintain, and that importantly costs less to build and operate.

Its arrival also comes amid a challenging time for Waymo, which recently suspended robotaxi service on freeways in Los Angeles, Miami, Phoenix, and San Francisco to improve how its vehicles behave in construction zones. Waymo also paused services in Atlanta, Georgia and San Antonio, Texas to address problems with flooding in those cities .
The launch of the blue-hued minivan might not wipe the slate clean for Waymo, but it does give the company a real chance at scale and revenue generation.
While the vehicle is loaded with Waymo’s hardware and software, its foundation comes from Zeekr, the brand owned by China’s Geely Holding Group.

The companies partnered in 2021 and showed off a concept of the purpose-built robotaxi in late 2022. Waymo has spent nearly two years testing the prototype, and later a production-intent version of the vehicle on public roads.

The minivan, which was designed in Sweden and manufactured in China, is based on the SEA-M architecture, a refined version of Zeekr’s original Sustainable Experience Architecture (SEA) meant for “future mobility products” like robotaxis and logistics vehicles.

The Ojai is equipped with Waymo’s sixth-generation system — including 13 cameras, four lidar sensors, six radar units, and an array of external audio receivers. That sixth-generation system is the keystone to Waymo’s commercial strategy because it’s designed to be modular. This means it can be applied to multiple kinds of vehicles, including two that have already been announced, the Zeekr minivan and the Hyundai Ioniq 5.

The Ojai is supposed to reflect the technological progress and lessons the company has learned from giving more than 500,000 paid robotaxi rides every week. And it’s also meant to accelerate the growth of Waymo’s fleet, which today is about 3,700 Jaguar I-Pace vehicles.

The stripped-down Zeekr vehicles — which don’t contain any Chinese connected car tech — are sent to Waymo’s Arizona factory, where they are outfitted with all of its robotaxi bells and whistles. The company said it is now scaling toward a capacity of tens of thousands of units annually starting with the Ojai, and followed by the Hyundai Ioniq 5.

The result is a vehicle with a flat floor, low step-in height, and gondola-like doors on both sides for easier entry and exit. There are other features aimed at pleasing riders, including charging ports, cup holders, increased leg and head room, grab bars, braille above various buttons, and three large adaptive screens, where customers can access the route, change music, control climate, and provide rider tips.
It also has an easier-to-clean interior, faster charging, a modular design, and increased battery capacity — all details that can help reduce costs and make maintenance and repairs more efficient.

sources.title: Waymo’s next robotaxi is a purpose-built Toyota bZ4X
passages: Waymo announced today that it will use Toyota bZ4X electric vehicles that are assembled in Japan for a robotaxi service in Tokyo.

And the company is working with Woven by Toyota, the automaker’s software and mobility spinout, to use Waymo’s operational and safety telemetry to improve road safety across general vehicle fleets and traffic infrastructure.
The news builds on the strategic partnership between Waymo and Toyota which was first announced in April 2025.

The decision to build the sensor suite and compute into the bZ4X on Toyota’s own assembly line could help eliminate redundant labor, bespoke brackets, and secondary shipping — and possibly bring down costs for Waymo.
Waymo also says it is continuing to explore integrating its technology into Toyota vehicles for personally owned autonomous vehicles.
The robotaxis will be built entirely under one roof at Toyota’s Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, Japan.
Instead of building regular cars and modifying them later, the factory will install Waymo’s self-driving sensors and computers right on the assembly line as each car is made.
Currently, Waymo uses two vehicle models on the road today — the Jaguar I-Pace and Ojai based on the Zeekr RT — with a third based on the Hyundai Ioniq 5 set to deploy soon.
By adding the bZ4X, Waymo is attempting to prove that its autonomous driving technology is compatible with a wide range of vehicle types.
Waymo has long positioned itself as a software and systems supplier — the “Waymo Driver” — rather than an automaker.
This also represents a shift in terms of how Waymo acquires and modifies the vehicles that end up in its fleet.

sources.title: Toyota to Launch 'bZ4X' Robotaxi Service in 2027 with Waymo Partnership, a First for Japan
passages: The 'bZ4X' robotaxi, equipped with Waymo's advanced autonomous driving hardware, undergoes all manufacturing processes—from basic vehicle assembly to the installation of dedicated hardware—exclusively at Toyota's Takaoka plant located in Aichi Prefecture, Japan.

Toyota Motor Corporation announced on the 30th that it will begin full-scale operations of an unmanned autonomous taxi based on its battery electric vehicle 'bZ4X' in 2027, in collaboration with U.S. self-driving technology company Waymo .

Toyota and Waymo plan to use the successful establishment of the service in the Japanese market as a stepping stone to gradually expand their cooperation into major global mobility markets, leading the standard for next-generation autonomous driving ecosystems.
This unmanned taxi service will be Japan's first fully autonomous commercial service utilizing mass-produced vehicles manufactured domestically within Japan.
Through this collaboration, the two companies plan to build a safer and more efficient unmanned mobility transportation network in urban driving environments within Japan .

passages: Waymo is adding the Toyota bZ4X to its robotaxi lineup.
Toyota will build a custom version of the electric SUV with the Waymo Driver integrated right on the line in Japan, and a test fleet will start operating there in 2027.
The UK and “other Waymo markets” come in later years, with no dates attached.
The timing lines up with Waymo’s Japan plans.

In September, Waymo said it’s targeting fully driverless commercial rides in Tokyo in 2027 with taxi operator Nihon Kotsu and ride-hailing app GO, scaling to about 100 vehicles, pending regulatory approval.
Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov said that “Toyota’s commitment to zero traffic accidents resonates deeply with us at Waymo.”
Yes, the bZ4X had a rough start (Toyota recalled the first batch in 2022 because the wheels could come off).
But it has come a long way now – becoming boring and reliable.

According to Waymo’s announcement , Toyota will produce the vehicles at its Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, and Waymo’s self-driving hardware will be installed and integrated at that same site instead of being retrofitted somewhere else.
It isn’t Toyota’s first robotaxi bZ4X either: Toyota and Pony.ai started mass-producing bZ4X-based robotaxis in China earlier this year.
In the US, Waymo’s fleet is still mostly made up of Jaguar I-Pace SUVs, a model Jaguar no longer produces.
It’s been adding the Zeekr-built Ojai van and the Hyundai Ioniq 5, and Hyundai is reportedly in talks to supply up to 50,000 Ioniq 5 robotaxis by 2028 .
Waymo’s biggest constraint right now is cars.
It has been running a fleet built on a discontinued Jaguar, and every new automaker it signs adds manufacturing capacity it doesn’t have to build itself.
Toyota is the world’s best-selling automaker.
Having it build Waymo-ready vehicles on its own assembly line is exactly the kind of industrial partner Waymo needed.
I believe it is simply a matter of time before it happens.
But what interests me most is the personal-vehicle angle.
Toyota and Waymo keep mentioning it, but there’s still nothing concrete.
Will that happen before the end of the decade?
When Waymo and Toyota first announced their deal in April 2025 , it was a preliminary agreement to “explore” working together on autonomous driving, including in personally owned vehicles.
The robotaxi bZ4X gets a few rider-focused changes: extra rear legroom, automatic doors, a power liftgate, and ambient lighting.
Waymo didn’t share sensor specs, unit volumes, or what each vehicle costs.
For US readers, the refreshed model is sold here simply as the Toyota bZ, starting at $34,900.
A cheap, high-volume base vehicle matters a lot when you’re trying to scale a fleet.
It’s the first actual vehicle to come out of the partnership the two companies signed last year.
Waymo keeps plugging its driver into existing EVs from established automakers and expanding city by city.

The timing lines up with Waymo’s Japan plans. In September, Waymo said it’s targeting fully driverless commercial rides in Tokyo in 2027 with taxi operator Nihon Kotsu and ride-hailing app GO, scaling to about 100 vehicles, pending regulatory approval.

The bZ4X makes four. It isn’t Toyota’s first robotaxi bZ4X either: Toyota and Pony.ai started mass-producing bZ4X-based robotaxis in China earlier this year.

And Waymo is scaling. It now does over 500,000 paid rides a week across 15 US metros, and it picked Toronto as its first Canadian city earlier this month, with riders targeted for 2028.
This is a big one, even if the bZ4X is about as exciting as a toaster.

Waymo’s biggest constraint right now is cars. It has been running a fleet built on a discontinued Jaguar, and every new automaker it signs adds manufacturing capacity it doesn’t have to build itself. Toyota is the world’s best-selling automaker. Having it build Waymo-ready vehicles on its own assembly line is exactly the kind of industrial partner Waymo needed.

Toyota and Waymo probably will follow through with offering the Waymo driver in personal vehicles, but it will probably take a while to get there, because of the need to map more roads. I believe it is simply a matter of time before it happens.

Yes, the bZ4X had a rough start (Toyota recalled the first batch in 2022 because the wheels could come off). But it has come a long way now – becoming boring and reliable. And for a robotaxi, boring and reliable is the whole point.

Waymo keeps plugging its driver into existing EVs from established automakers and expanding city by city. So far, that’s working.

The way it is looking now. It sounds like Toyota will take over manufacturing Waymo driver cars for right-hand-drive markets. But what interests me most is the personal-vehicle angle. Toyota and Waymo keep mentioning it, but there’s still nothing concrete. If Toyota actually puts the Waymo Driver in a car you can buy, Tesla’s FSD Supervised pitch gets a lot harder to sell. Will that happen before the end of the decade? Who knows.
