extraction.body: Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what is thought to be the biggest crypto hack on record. The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses". The company said while initial checks suggested an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, "our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach". Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor. Cyber-security firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack. Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record". AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack. The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen. The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added. Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide. The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under its custody. The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world. Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack. For the last few years North Korea-linked operatives have focussed on attacking cryptocurrency companies for large thefts of digital tokens. Eric Jardine, Chainalysis' Head of Research, urged every exchange to remain vigilant as the platforms are attractive targets for hackers due to the sheer value of assets. Binance did not directly respond to BBC questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice." The incident concerns Binance.com - while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US, which provides trading services specifically for American residents - said its platform is not affected by the issue. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the company's initial investigation suggested the hack started with a compromised engineer's laptop. "That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions," he said in a statement. In an update, the company said in a statement on X that another investigation found there had been other breach points: "We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them." Check Point's Dave said this attack also resembled a hack on crypto exchange platform Bitget in September in which $388m (£289m) was lost: "This implies that attackers no longer need the vault keys. They target the systems and people with authority to use them." In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets. "Safety first: withdrawals are currently disabled until the environment is confirmed to be secure," she said. Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they had frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack. World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it has worked with its partners to freeze stolen funds. Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation. Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue. Bitcoin dropped by more than 4% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply. The cyber-attack, which the company describes as complex, is believed to be the largest ever of its kind. Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said his firm has frozen around $1.6bn "related to a potential Binance exchange hack." Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue. The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen. AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack. Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide. Binance did not directly respond to BBC queries about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice." Early checks show the incident may have involved an engineer's laptop that had been compromised, which allowed an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said. Chainalysis, another crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack. Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation. In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets.

extraction.body: Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what could be the largest hack in history. The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses". Early checks show the incident may have involved an engineer's laptop that had been compromised, which allowed an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said. Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor. AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack. The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen. The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added. Chainalysis, another crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack. For the last few years North Korea-linked operatives have focussed on attacking cryptocurrency companies for large thefts of digital tokens. Western security agencies have previously said stolen funds are used to finance North Korea's nuclear weapons and missile development programs. The regime has denied any involvement in hacks in the past. Eric Jardine, Chainalysis' Head of Research, urged every exchange to remain vigilant as the platforms are attractive targets for hackers due to the sheer value of assets. Binance did not directly respond to BBC queries about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice." The incident concerns Binance.com - while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US, which provides trading services specifically for American residents - said its platform is not affected by the issue. In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets. "Safety first: withdrawals are currently disabled until the environment is confirmed to be secure," she said. Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they have frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack. Circle chief executive Jeremy Allaire said his firm is "closely tracking reports of a potential exploit involving Binance" and that his company has frozen more than $800m in assets linked to the incident. Circle is the issuer and co-creator of the USDC, one of the world's largest US dollar-backed cryptocurrencies. Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said his firm has frozen around $1.6bn "related to a potential Binance exchange hack." "Protecting the industry and our partners is our main priority," said Ardoino, whose company issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT. World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it has worked with its partners to freeze stolen funds. Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation. Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue. Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide. The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world. The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under custody. Bitcoin dropped by more than 4% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.

The company said while initial checks suggested an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, "our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach". Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor. Cybersecurity firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack. Check Point's chief information security officer, Jayant Dave, said the losses Binance estimated made it "the largest crypto theft on record". AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack. The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen. The attacker still holds a massive sum of stolen assets, so efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added. Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide. In 2024, the company said it has more than $160bn in assets under its custody. The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world. Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack. For the last few years North Korea-linked operatives have focussed on attacking cryptocurrency companies for large thefts of digital tokens. Eric Jardine, Chainalysis' Head of Research, urged every exchange to remain vigilant as the platforms are attractive targets for hackers due to the sheer value of assets. Binance did not directly respond to BBC questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice." The incident concerns Binance.com - while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US, which provides trading services specifically for American residents - said its platform is not affected by the issue. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the company's initial investigation suggested the hack started with a compromised engineer's laptop. "That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorised withdrawal transactions," he said in a statement. "To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual. So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak." He said a detailed "post-mortem" would be shared once the investigation was complete. In an update, the company said in a statement on X that another investigation found there had been other breach points: "We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them." Check Point's Dave said this attack also resembled a hack on crypto exchange platform Bitget in September in which $388m (£289m) was lost: "This implies that attackers no longer need the vault keys. They target the systems and people with authority to use them." In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets. "Safety first: withdrawals are currently disabled until the environment is confirmed to be secure," she said. Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they had frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack. World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it has worked with its partners to freeze stolen funds. Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation. Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue. Bitcoin dropped by more than 4% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.

extraction.body: Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what is thought to be the biggest crypto hack on record. The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses". The company said while initial checks suggested an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, "our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach". Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor. Cyber-security firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack. Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record". AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack. The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen. The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added. Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide. The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under its custody. The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world. Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack. For the last few years North Korea-linked operatives have focussed on attacking cryptocurrency companies for large thefts of digital tokens. Eric Jardine, Chainalysis' Head of Research, urged every exchange to remain vigilant as the platforms are attractive targets for hackers due to the sheer value of assets. Binance did not directly respond to BBC questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice." The incident concerns Binance.com - while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US, which provides trading services specifically for American residents - said its platform is not affected by the issue. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the company's initial investigation suggested the hack started with a compromised engineer's laptop. "That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions," he said in a statement. In an update, the company said in a statement on X that another investigation found there had been other breach points: "We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them." Check Point's Dave said this attack also resembled a hack on crypto exchange platform Bitget in September in which $388m (£289m) was lost: "This implies that attackers no longer need the vault keys. They target the systems and people with authority to use them." In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets. "Safety first: withdrawals are currently disabled until the environment is confirmed to be secure," she said. Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they had frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack. World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it has worked with its partners to freeze stolen funds. Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation. Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue. Bitcoin dropped by more than 4% following the alerts. The exchange, Binance, announced late Thursday that more than $6 billion appeared to have moved through wallets connected to a security breach. It did not appear that the hackers were able to access customer accounts or holdings. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng released a video statement Friday morning that sought to reassure platform users. "Your assets are safe," he said, adding "we never use customer funds, so they are not impacted." Instead, Binance's corporate holdings were affected, he said. The company said it had set aside $5 billion to cover the losses and was working with partners to purchase an additional $1.34 billion in cryptocurrencies to cover the total amount believed to have been stolen. In a statement, the Secret Service said it was working with private-sector partners, including U.S.-based crypto group Circle, to identify, freeze, trace and recover funds stolen from Binance. It also said it was coordinating with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia and other law enforcement partners to identify those responsible. It said its investigation remained in early stages. The hack is the latest setback for crypto, which continues to reckon with a reputation for being too volatile — and too vulnerable to criminal activity — for widespread use. The scale of the hack echoes collapse of crypto exchange FTX, which, though not the result of a cyberattack, caused billions in losses. The renewed doubts were reflected in Bitcoin's value Friday, which fell more than 5% overnight to approximately $77,000, accelerating its month-long downturn. Other affected cryptocurrencies fell as much as 9%. The crypto industry was already reeling from the failure in Congress of the Clarity Act, a bill that would have granted comprehensive legal protections for crypto assets in the U.S. Despite bipartisan support for the core elements of the legislation, its passage was torpedoed by a battle over conflict-of-interest rules for elected officials, notably President Donald Trump. The president has disclosed in filings that he earned more than $1 billion from crypto last year. The Binance hack stands to prolong this reckoning, experts said. "There will be an imperative for Binance to cover losses not only for its own reputation and value, but I expect there will be a level of co-operation within the space as they look at the collective reputational harm this may, rightly or wrongly, cause to the sector," Laura Clatworthy, head of digital assets at the law firm Edwin Coe, said in a statement. That cooperation was seen in the immediate reaction of other mainstream crypto players. Crypto firms Tether and Circle, which operate the two-largest stablecoins, worked quickly to freeze assets implicated in the hack. However, U.S. blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs estimates that $2.4 billion in Bitcoin and Ethereum will never be recovered. As of Friday morning, the hack's origins remained murky. The whole heist unfolded in just 20 minutes starting at approximately 4 p.m. ET Thursday. Binance initially said the attack involved a compromised laptop. "However, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," ‌it said in a statement on X, without elaborating. Multiple blockchain analysis firms said the hack had attributes associated with previous operations believed to have been carried out by North Korean actors. Teng, the Binance co-CEO, said Binance's investigation had not yet identified the attackers. At least one prominent tech CEO could not resist making light of the situation. Elon Musk left a "yikes" emoji in response to an X user who noted that the collapsed crypto exchange FTX had initially also told users their funds were safe amid a wave of losses. Binance co-founder CZ Zhao responded:"Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop." Zhao noted that his SpaceX shares — the product of a Binance-related $500 million investment in Twitter, were now worth more than $1 billion. "Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!" sources.title: North Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’ - The Guardian
passages: The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.
Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers.
TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis.
North Korea, a state hampered by sanctions and starved for cash, has become a prolific hacker of crypto, an asset it favours because it can be stolen in bulk and laundered.
The regime has stolen more than $6.5bn in crypto assets in recent years, including more than $1bn so far in 2026, according to Elliptic.
Q&A: How big a deal is the $6.3bn crypto heist?
Researchers said the theft was the biggest ever, dwarfing a $1.5bn crypto raid last year and the $1bn taken from Iraq’s central bank by Saddam Hussein in 2003 .
“This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic.

Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks.

Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.

World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.

While crypto companies are not regulated in the UK, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will be keeping an eye on any banks, insurers or fintechs that are exposed to Binance, and how that could hurt the UK’s wider financial system.

An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and ⁠make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said.
Zhao posted to X on Thursday: “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack”.
Tell us: have you been affected by the Binance hack?
Binance exchange says it will cover customer losses as it scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so far
In a post on X, Binance reiterated that it was working “to trace, freeze and recover additional funds”, and signed off: “We will weather this storm.

Binance said it would cover all losses and that users' funds are safe. A massive hack of Binance is sending shockwaves through digital assets and crypto-linked stocks on Friday. Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, said on Friday that a compromised engineer's laptop may have allowed hackers to gain access to the platform. It said that $6.3 billion of assets were impacted. The news sent crypto prices down across the board, with Bitcoin , Ethereum , Solana all falling at least 4% Friday morning while and BNB, the native crypto of the Binance ecosystem, fell 6.5%. Crypto-linked stocks were also pulled down. Bitcoin's drop to around $76,700 puts it at its lowest level in a month. "The market is currently undergoing a crucial test of buyer sentiment," said Alex Kuptsikevich, chief market analyst at FxPro. "In theory, we could see a wave of sell-offs due to a reassessment of risks facing the sector." As of Friday morning, more than $3 billion in crypto assets are currently frozen on-chain as the company maneuvers quickly to cover the damage caused by the hack. The largest crypto theft to date, it is already viewed as one of the most significant financial heists on record. The most recent similarly sized hack occurred in February 2025, when North Korean hackers made off with $1.5 billion in crypto assets from Dubai exchange platform Bybit. The immediate market impact of Friday's cyber attack has been a quick risk-off wave washing over the space. Digital security pros also say that more attacks of this magnitude are possible, which could compel investors to move assets off of exchanges or simply exit crypto markets altogether. "A cyber attack of this level is a matter of when, not if, particularly alongside the rise of AI," said Andy Ward, SVP International at Absolute Security. "Cyber threats are becoming more sophisticated and widespread as ever, and it is likely only a matter of time before an even larger hack, with even greater financial fallout, makes headlines." extraction.body: A record-setting cyberattack targeting the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange rocked the digital assets industry Friday, delivering another blow to a sector already struggling to achieve mainstream adoption. The exchange, Binance, announced late Thursday that more than $6 billion appeared to have moved through wallets connected to a security breach. Around $3 billion of that had potentially been located and frozen across several exchanges, though it was not immediately clear if those funds were recoverable. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng released a video statement Friday morning that sought to reassure platform users. “Your assets are safe,” he said, adding “we never use customer funds, so they are not impacted.” Instead, Binance’s corporate holdings were affected, he said. The company said it had set aside $5 billion to cover the losses and was working with partners to purchase an additional $1.34 billion in cryptocurrencies to cover the total amount believed to have been stolen. In a statement, the Secret Service said it was working with private-sector partners, including U.S.-based crypto group Circle, to identify, freeze, trace and recover funds stolen from Binance. It also said it was coordinating with the U.S. It said its investigation remained in early stages. The hack is the latest setback for crypto, which continues to reckon with a reputation for being too volatile — and too vulnerable to criminal activity — for widespread use. The scale of the hack echoes collapse of crypto exchange FTX, which, though not the result of a cyberattack, caused billions in losses. The crypto industry was already reeling from the failure in Congress of the Clarity Act, a bill that would have granted comprehensive legal protections for crypto assets in the U.S. The president has disclosed in filings that he earned more than $1 billion from crypto last year. The Binance hack stands to prolong this reckoning, experts said. “There will be an imperative for Binance to cover losses not only for its own reputation and value, but I expect there will be a level of co-operation within the space as they look at the collective reputational harm this may, rightly or wrongly, cause to the sector,” Laura Clatworthy, head of digital assets at the law firm Edwin Coe, said in a statement. That cooperation was seen in the immediate reaction of other mainstream crypto players. Crypto firms Tether and Circle, which operate the two-largest stablecoins, worked quickly to freeze assets implicated in the hack. However, U.S. blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs estimates that $2.4 billion in Bitcoin and Ethereum will never be recovered. As of Friday morning, the hack’s origins remained murky. Binance initially said the attack involved a compromised laptop. “However, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” ‌it said in a statement on X, without elaborating. Multiple blockchain analysis firms said the hack had attributes associated with previous operations believed to have been carried out by North Korean actors. Teng, the Binance co-CEO, said Binance’s investigation had not yet identified the attackers. At least one prominent tech CEO could not resist making light of the situation. Elon Musk left a “yikes” emoji in response to an X user who noted that the collapsed crypto exchange FTX had initially also told users their funds were safe amid a wave of losses. Binance co-founder CZ Zhao responded:“Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop.” Zhao noted that his SpaceX shares — the product of a Binance-related $500 million investment in Twitter, were now worth more than $1 billion.

The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.
Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers.
TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis.
North Korea, a state hampered by sanctions and starved for cash, has become a prolific hacker of crypto, an asset it favours because it can be stolen in bulk and laundered.
The regime has stolen more than $6.5bn in crypto assets in recent years, including more than $1bn so far in 2026, according to Elliptic.
Q&A: How big a deal is the $6.3bn crypto heist?
Researchers said the theft was the biggest ever, dwarfing a $1.5bn crypto raid last year and the $1bn taken from Iraq’s central bank by Saddam Hussein in 2003 .
“This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic.

Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks.

In a statement, the Secret Service said it was working with private-sector partners, including U.S.-based crypto group Circle, to identify, freeze, trace and recover funds stolen from Binance. It also said it was coordinating with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia and other law enforcement partners to identify those responsible. It said its investigation remained in early stages. The hack is the latest setback for crypto, which continues to reckon with a reputation for being too volatile — and too vulnerable to criminal activity — for widespread use. The scale of the hack echoes collapse of crypto exchange FTX, which, though not the result of a cyberattack, caused billions in losses. The renewed doubts were reflected in Bitcoin's value Friday, which fell more than 5% overnight to approximately $77,000, accelerating its month-long downturn. Other affected cryptocurrencies fell as much as 9%. The crypto industry was already reeling from the failure in Congress of the Clarity Act, a bill that would have granted comprehensive legal protections for crypto assets in the U.S. Despite bipartisan support for the core elements of the legislation, its passage was torpedoed by a battle over conflict-of-interest rules for elected officials, notably President Donald Trump. extraction.body: A record-setting cyberattack targeting the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange rocked the digital assets industry Friday, delivering another blow to a sector already struggling to achieve mainstream adoption. The exchange, Binance, announced late Thursday that more than $6 billion appeared to have moved through wallets connected to a security breach. Around $3 billion of that had potentially been located and frozen across several exchanges, though it was not immediately clear if those funds were recoverable. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng released a video statement Friday morning that sought to reassure platform users. “Your assets are safe,” he said, adding “we never use customer funds, so they are not impacted.” Instead, Binance’s corporate holdings were affected, he said. The company said it had set aside $5 billion to cover the losses and was working with partners to purchase an additional $1.34 billion in cryptocurrencies to cover the total amount believed to have been stolen. In a statement, the Secret Service said it was working with private-sector partners, including U.S.-based crypto group Circle, to identify, freeze, trace and recover funds stolen from Binance. It also said it was coordinating with the U.S. It said its investigation remained in early stages. The hack is the latest setback for crypto, which continues to reckon with a reputation for being too volatile — and too vulnerable to criminal activity — for widespread use. The scale of the hack echoes collapse of crypto exchange FTX, which, though not the result of a cyberattack, caused billions in losses. The crypto industry was already reeling from the failure in Congress of the Clarity Act, a bill that would have granted comprehensive legal protections for crypto assets in the U.S. The president has disclosed in filings that he earned more than $1 billion from crypto last year. The Binance hack stands to prolong this reckoning, experts said. “There will be an imperative for Binance to cover losses not only for its own reputation and value, but I expect there will be a level of co-operation within the space as they look at the collective reputational harm this may, rightly or wrongly, cause to the sector,” Laura Clatworthy, head of digital assets at the law firm Edwin Coe, said in a statement. That cooperation was seen in the immediate reaction of other mainstream crypto players. Crypto firms Tether and Circle, which operate the two-largest stablecoins, worked quickly to freeze assets implicated in the hack. However, U.S. blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs estimates that $2.4 billion in Bitcoin and Ethereum will never be recovered. As of Friday morning, the hack’s origins remained murky. Binance initially said the attack involved a compromised laptop. “However, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” ‌it said in a statement on X, without elaborating. Multiple blockchain analysis firms said the hack had attributes associated with previous operations believed to have been carried out by North Korean actors. Teng, the Binance co-CEO, said Binance’s investigation had not yet identified the attackers. At least one prominent tech CEO could not resist making light of the situation. Elon Musk left a “yikes” emoji in response to an X user who noted that the collapsed crypto exchange FTX had initially also told users their funds were safe amid a wave of losses. Binance co-founder CZ Zhao responded:“Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop.” Zhao noted that his SpaceX shares — the product of a Binance-related $500 million investment in Twitter, were now worth more than $1 billion.

extraction.body: Binance scrambles to freeze billions after record-breaking hack linked to North Korea. Binance has suspended all withdrawals after the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange fell victim to what appears to be the biggest heist in history. The exchange put the “estimated total impact” of the hack at about $6.3 billion and said around $3 billion of affected assets, mainly stablecoins that act as cash for the crypto market, had been frozen. But analysts at Elliptic said the attacker had changed about $3.3 billion into digital assets that could not be frozen and was working to cash those out as traditional currency. An “initial investigation” suggested hackers had been able to compromise an engineer’s laptop and withdraw funds from the platform, Binance said, adding on Friday morning that further investigation “has uncovered additional points of breach.” The company is working with law enforcement. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs linked the hack with a North Korean unit known as TraderTraitor, saying that the sums involved would make it “the largest crypto theft on record.” Last year, North Korean hackers stole crypto worth $1.5 billion in an attack on exchange Bybit. Peter Ward, of the Sejong Institute in Seoul, said North Korea had considerable expertise and offered “near-total protection to its hackers.” “Things may get a lot worse going forward,” he said. Binance said on Friday that it had “already reserved over $6.34 billion of company funds to cover this incident,” with $5 billion of the funds “already held in the exact token assets that were impacted.” The company said it was actively buying more tokens in order to cover the remaining amount. “This step can take longer because some tokens may have low liquidity,” and settlement “also takes time,” it said. The hack is a major blow to Binance, which was co-founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao and holds about $140 billion of digital assets. In 2023, the company pleaded guilty to US criminal charges related to breach of anti-money laundering laws and paid a $4.3 billion fine. Zhao, known as CZ, pleaded guilty to criminal charges relating to inadequate money laundering controls. He stepped down as chief executive and was pardoned last year by US President Donald Trump. The crypto market is in the grip of a prolonged downturn after a sharp sell-off late last year wiped more than $1tn from the combined capitalization of about 18,000 digital tokens. Richard Teng, co-chief executive of Binance, told customers that their “money is safe, and we’re covering every loss” from a reserve fund as well as “company funds.” Binance’s reserve fund holds about $1 billion worth of bitcoin, according to a company update from mid-October. Zhao said this leaves roughly $2 billion that the company still needs to cover, adding that the company owns shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX worth more than $1 billion. “Remaining gap is (still painful, but) manageable,” he said in a post on X. Binance co-chief executive Yi He said on Friday that the company’s annual revenue “is sufficient to cover the losses,” without giving further details. CZ said earlier this year that the company’s annual revenue is about $5 billion. Crypto venues have become lucrative targets for hackers, with notable heists including $280 million stolen in April from the coffers of unregulated crypto exchange Drift. Unlike traditional exchanges, crypto venues sit on big piles of customer assets. Some institutional investors in recent years have sought third-party custody arrangements in order to keep their funds elsewhere and mitigate the risks of their assets being stolen directly off the exchange. Binance works with Swiss banks Sygnum and Flow, the FT previously reported. Abu Dhabi’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which regulates Binance’s main global crypto exchange, said in a statement on Friday that it was aware of the “security incident involving unauthorized withdrawals of assets” from the company’s exchange and was “engaging closely with Binance.” Binance was ordered to wind down its EU operations in July after it failed to secure a license under the bloc’s new regulatory framework. The exchange, which became regulated in Abu Dhabi in December 2025, had already agreed to block UK customers from signing up for the exchange after being barred by Britain’s financial watchdog in 2021. In the US, Binance operates under a separate entity from the rest of its global operations that is registered with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network and authorized to operate as a money transmitter in 32 states. Last month, nearly $390 million was stolen from crypto exchange Bitget, which reimbursed customers from its so-called User Protection Fund. North Korean hackers stole about $2 billion in cryptocurrency in 2025, a 50 percent increase from the year before, according to data from Chainalysis. Binance said it found no evidence that unique user codes, known as “private keys,” had been breached. In a post on X early on Friday, Yi He said the exchange expected to allow withdrawals again “in the next 48 hours.” Binance, which has no official headquarters, last year became regulated in Abu Dhabi, where Zhao and He, who are romantic partners, are based. In a sign of the potential repercussions from the heist, Paolo Ardoino, chief executive of Tether, said his company had frozen about $1.5 billion of USDT, its $180 billion dollar-linked stablecoin. Jeremy Allaire, head of Circle, the second-biggest stablecoin issuer, said $800 million of its USDC coin had been frozen amid “reports of a potential exploit” at Binance. Crypto companies can freeze the wallets in which stolen funds are moved or held. Analytics firm Elliptic said it had verified $2.8 billion of frozen crypto—mostly USDT and USDC—but that the hackers had moved the remainder into assets that could not be frozen, such as the ETH crypto token. “This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” Elliptic said.

REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration By Lawrence Delevingne, Summer Zhen and Elizabeth Howcroft BOSTON/SINGAPORE/PARIS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a theft that analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time. Cryptocurrency prices fell on the news, while Binance halted withdrawals and said it would use company funds to cover the losses. Stablecoin issuers including El Salvador-based Tether and the Trump-backed World Liberty Financial froze about half of the stolen assets. The exchange said customer funds were safe and it was working with partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It said earlier on Friday it expected to resume withdrawal services in the next 48 hours. It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion, but Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a post on X that $3 billion represented only about 2% of the company's total user assets and public reserves. Binance said it had set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1 billion. Binance other co-CEO, Richard Teng, said in a post on X that the breach as a "complex attack" that was not carried out by one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity as it went along, "making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate." The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called "hot" wallet in a way that did not pass through normal approval controls, Teng said. "Rest assured that we are working non-stop to resolve this, to make the users whole, and live up to your trust," Teng wrote. The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. "This incident is almost certainly the single largest known theft of any kind," British blockchain analysts Elliptic said. The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis. TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea. North Korea has âfor years â used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well â as cybersecurity âexperts. North Korea routinely denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment. "When North Korea steals at this scale, the money supports weapons proliferation, which makes this a national security issue, not just a crypto theft," Ari Redbord, global head of policy and government affairs at TRM, said. Binance is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the United States Secret Service (USSS), a person familiar with the situation told Reuters. The FBI said it was "aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps." The USSS said in a statement that its investigators "are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle, to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday." Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million. Abu Dhabi's Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance's main operating licence, said it was "engaging closely with Binance and monitoring the incident". Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX declined to comment. It became a minority investor in Binance last year. Crypto prices fell broadly but losses were contained. Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the crypto sector, which had already been under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said. "It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group. Investor Michael Saylor, among Bitcoin's most prominent supporters, said in a post on X that he expected Binance to "deliver" on ensuring no customers suffered losses. "Our industry will learn from this incident, strengthen security, and emerge stronger and more resilient," he wrote on Friday. Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report. By Lawrence Delevingne, Summer Zhen and Elizabeth Howcroft

BOSTON/SINGAPORE/PARIS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a theft that analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time.

Cryptocurrency prices fell on the news, while Binance halted withdrawals and said it would use company funds to cover the losses. Stablecoin issuers including El Salvador-based Tether and the Trump-backed World Liberty Financial froze about half of the stolen assets.

The exchange said customer funds were safe and it was working with partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It said earlier on Friday it expected to resume withdrawal services in the next 48 hours. It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion, but Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a post on X that $3 billion represented only about 2% of the company's total user assets and public reserves.

Binance said it had set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1 billion.

Binance other co-CEO, Richard Teng, said in a post on X that the breach as a "complex attack" that was not carried out by one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity as it went along, "making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate."

The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called "hot" wallet in a way that did not pass through normal approval controls, Teng said.
"Rest assured that we are working non-stop to resolve this, to make the users whole, and live up to your trust," Teng wrote.
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
"This incident is almost certainly the single largest known theft of any kind," British blockchain analysts Elliptic said.

The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea.
North Korea has âfor years â used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well â as cybersecurity âexperts.
North Korea routinely denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment.

"When North Korea steals at this scale, the money supports weapons proliferation, which makes this a national security issue, not just a crypto theft," Ari Redbord, global head of policy and government affairs at TRM, said.
Binance is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the United States Secret Service (USSS), a person familiar with the situation told Reuters.

The FBI said it was "aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps."

The USSS said in a statement that its investigators "are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle, to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday."
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.

Abu Dhabi's Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance's main operating licence, said it was "engaging closely with Binance and monitoring the incident". Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX declined to comment. It became a minority investor in Binance last year.
Crypto prices fell broadly but losses were contained.

Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the crypto sector, which had already been under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
"It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group.

Investor Michael Saylor, among Bitcoin's most prominent supporters, said in a post on X that he expected Binance to "deliver" on ensuring no customers suffered losses. "Our industry will learn from this incident, strengthen security, and emerge stronger and more resilient," he wrote on Friday.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.

extraction.body: Binance scrambles to freeze billions after record-breaking hack linked to North Korea. Binance has suspended all withdrawals after the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange fell victim to what appears to be the biggest heist in history. The exchange put the “estimated total impact” of the hack at about $6.3 billion and said around $3 billion of affected assets, mainly stablecoins that act as cash for the crypto market, had been frozen. But analysts at Elliptic said the attacker had changed about $3.3 billion into digital assets that could not be frozen and was working to cash those out as traditional currency. An “initial investigation” suggested hackers had been able to compromise an engineer’s laptop and withdraw funds from the platform, Binance said, adding on Friday morning that further investigation “has uncovered additional points of breach.” The company is working with law enforcement. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs linked the hack with a North Korean unit known as TraderTraitor, saying that the sums involved would make it “the largest crypto theft on record.” Last year, North Korean hackers stole crypto worth $1.5 billion in an attack on exchange Bybit. Peter Ward, of the Sejong Institute in Seoul, said North Korea had considerable expertise and offered “near-total protection to its hackers.” “Things may get a lot worse going forward,” he said. Binance said on Friday that it had “already reserved over $6.34 billion of company funds to cover this incident,” with $5 billion of the funds “already held in the exact token assets that were impacted.” The company said it was actively buying more tokens in order to cover the remaining amount. “This step can take longer because some tokens may have low liquidity,” and settlement “also takes time,” it said. The hack is a major blow to Binance, which was co-founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao and holds about $140 billion of digital assets. In 2023, the company pleaded guilty to US criminal charges related to breach of anti-money laundering laws and paid a $4.3 billion fine. Zhao, known as CZ, pleaded guilty to criminal charges relating to inadequate money laundering controls. He stepped down as chief executive and was pardoned last year by US President Donald Trump. The crypto market is in the grip of a prolonged downturn after a sharp sell-off late last year wiped more than $1tn from the combined capitalization of about 18,000 digital tokens. Richard Teng, co-chief executive of Binance, told customers that their “money is safe, and we’re covering every loss” from a reserve fund as well as “company funds.” Binance’s reserve fund holds about $1 billion worth of bitcoin, according to a company update from mid-October. Zhao said this leaves roughly $2 billion that the company still needs to cover, adding that the company owns shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX worth more than $1 billion. “Remaining gap is (still painful, but) manageable,” he said in a post on X. Binance co-chief executive Yi He said on Friday that the company’s annual revenue “is sufficient to cover the losses,” without giving further details. CZ said earlier this year that the company’s annual revenue is about $5 billion. Crypto venues have become lucrative targets for hackers, with notable heists including $280 million stolen in April from the coffers of unregulated crypto exchange Drift. Unlike traditional exchanges, crypto venues sit on big piles of customer assets. Some institutional investors in recent years have sought third-party custody arrangements in order to keep their funds elsewhere and mitigate the risks of their assets being stolen directly off the exchange. Binance works with Swiss banks Sygnum and Flow, the FT previously reported. Abu Dhabi’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which regulates Binance’s main global crypto exchange, said in a statement on Friday that it was aware of the “security incident involving unauthorized withdrawals of assets” from the company’s exchange and was “engaging closely with Binance.” Binance was ordered to wind down its EU operations in July after it failed to secure a license under the bloc’s new regulatory framework. The exchange, which became regulated in Abu Dhabi in December 2025, had already agreed to block UK customers from signing up for the exchange after being barred by Britain’s financial watchdog in 2021. In the US, Binance operates under a separate entity from the rest of its global operations that is registered with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network and authorized to operate as a money transmitter in 32 states. Last month, nearly $390 million was stolen from crypto exchange Bitget, which reimbursed customers from its so-called User Protection Fund. North Korean hackers stole about $2 billion in cryptocurrency in 2025, a 50 percent increase from the year before, according to data from Chainalysis. Binance said it found no evidence that unique user codes, known as “private keys,” had been breached. In a post on X early on Friday, Yi He said the exchange expected to allow withdrawals again “in the next 48 hours.” Binance, which has no official headquarters, last year became regulated in Abu Dhabi, where Zhao and He, who are romantic partners, are based. In a sign of the potential repercussions from the heist, Paolo Ardoino, chief executive of Tether, said his company had frozen about $1.5 billion of USDT, its $180 billion dollar-linked stablecoin. Jeremy Allaire, head of Circle, the second-biggest stablecoin issuer, said $800 million of its USDC coin had been frozen amid “reports of a potential exploit” at Binance. Crypto companies can freeze the wallets in which stolen funds are moved or held. Analytics firm Elliptic said it had verified $2.8 billion of frozen crypto—mostly USDT and USDC—but that the hackers had moved the remainder into assets that could not be frozen, such as the ETH crypto token. “This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” Elliptic said.

REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration By Lawrence Delevingne, Summer Zhen and Elizabeth Howcroft BOSTON/SINGAPORE/PARIS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a theft that analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time. Cryptocurrency prices fell on the news, while Binance halted withdrawals and said it would use company funds to cover the losses. Stablecoin issuers including El Salvador-based Tether and the Trump-backed World Liberty Financial froze about half of the stolen assets. The exchange said customer funds were safe and it was working with partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It said earlier on Friday it expected to resume withdrawal services in the next 48 hours. It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion, but Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a post on X that $3 billion represented only about 2% of the company's total user assets and public reserves. Binance said it had set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1 billion. Binance other co-CEO, Richard Teng, said in a post on X that the breach as a "complex attack" that was not carried out by one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity as it went along, "making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate." The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called "hot" wallet in a way that did not pass through normal approval controls, Teng said. "Rest assured that we are working non-stop to resolve this, to make the users whole, and live up to your trust," Teng wrote. The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. "This incident is almost certainly the single largest known theft of any kind," British blockchain analysts Elliptic said. The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis. TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea. North Korea has âfor years â used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well â as cybersecurity âexperts. North Korea routinely denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment. "When North Korea steals at this scale, the money supports weapons proliferation, which makes this a national security issue, not just a crypto theft," Ari Redbord, global head of policy and government affairs at TRM, said. Binance is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the United States Secret Service (USSS), a person familiar with the situation told Reuters. The FBI said it was "aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps." The USSS said in a statement that its investigators "are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle, to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday." Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million. Abu Dhabi's Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance's main operating licence, said it was "engaging closely with Binance and monitoring the incident". Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX declined to comment. It became a minority investor in Binance last year. Crypto prices fell broadly but losses were contained. Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the crypto sector, which had already been under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said. "It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group. Investor Michael Saylor, among Bitcoin's most prominent supporters, said in a post on X that he expected Binance to "deliver" on ensuring no customers suffered losses. "Our industry will learn from this incident, strengthen security, and emerge stronger and more resilient," he wrote on Friday. By Lawrence Delevingne, Summer Zhen and Elizabeth Howcroft BOSTON/SINGAPORE/PARIS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a theft
FILE PHOTO: Representations of cryptocurrencies are seen in front of displayed Binance logo in this illustration taken November 10, 2022. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration/File Photo
Smartphone with displayed Binance logo and representation of cryptocurrencies are placed on a keyboard in this illustration taken, June 8, 2023. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration
By Lawrence Delevingne, Summer Zhen and Elizabeth Howcroft

BOSTON/SINGAPORE/PARIS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a theft that analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time.

Cryptocurrency prices fell on the news, while Binance halted withdrawals and said it would use company funds to cover the losses. Stablecoin issuers including El Salvador-based Tether and the Trump-backed World Liberty Financial froze about half of the stolen assets.

The exchange said customer funds were safe and it was working with partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It said earlier on Friday it expected to resume withdrawal services in the next 48 hours. It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion, but Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a post on X that $3 billion represented only about 2% of the company's total user assets and public reserves.

Binance said it had set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1 billion.

Binance other co-CEO, Richard Teng, said in a post on X that the breach as a "complex attack" that was not carried out by one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity as it went along, "making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate."

The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called "hot" wallet in a way that did not pass through normal approval controls, Teng said.
"Rest assured that we are working non-stop to resolve this, to make the users whole, and live up to your trust," Teng wrote.
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
"This incident is almost certainly the single largest known theft of any kind," British blockchain analysts Elliptic said.

The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea.
North Korea has âfor years â used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well â as cybersecurity âexperts.
North Korea routinely denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment.

"When North Korea steals at this scale, the money supports weapons proliferation, which makes this a national security issue, not just a crypto theft," Ari Redbord, global head of policy and government affairs at TRM, said.
Binance is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the United States Secret Service (USSS), a person familiar with the situation told Reuters.

The FBI said it was "aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps."

The USSS said in a statement that its investigators "are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle, to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday."
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.

Abu Dhabi's Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance's main operating licence, said it was "engaging closely with Binance and monitoring the incident". Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX declined to comment. It became a minority investor in Binance last year.
Crypto prices fell broadly but losses were contained.

Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the crypto sector, which had already been under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
"It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group.

Investor Michael Saylor, among Bitcoin's most prominent supporters, said in a post on X that he expected Binance to "deliver" on ensuring no customers suffered losses. "Our industry will learn from this incident, strengthen security, and emerge stronger and more resilient," he wrote on Friday.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.

passages: North Korean hackers are suspected of carrying out a record-breaking $6.3 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, according to US-based blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs.

The firm said: “An attacker moved approximately $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes.” Explaining its assessment of the perpetrators, TRM added: “TRM attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, based on robust on and off-chain intelligence.

ALSO READ: ‘Tejashwi + Prashant Kishor’: Lalu's Daughter Rohini Acharya Floats New Formula To Counter BJP In Bihar Crypto Firms Freeze Billions As Hacker Moves Funds Several cryptocurrency companies and blockchain networks intervened to restrict access to the stolen assets.

TRM reported: “Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial froze about USD 2.67 billion in stablecoins, and Arbitrum’s Security Council froze 8,426 ETH and 74.6 million ARB on its network, for a total of roughly USD 2.7 billion.” However, the attacker allegedly attempted to move funds before further restrictions could be imposed.

According to TRM, the hacker “raced the freezes by selling USDT to market makers and borrowing ETH against USDT on Aave.” The attacker was subsequently holding more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth approximately $2.4 billion, which TRM described as assets beyond the reach of issuers capable of freezing them.
We make this judgment with high confidence.” If confirmed, the incident would be the biggest cryptocurrency theft recorded so far.
The previous record was the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025.

extraction.body: SINGAPORE/PARIS/BOSTON: Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a theft that analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time. Cryptocurrency prices fell ​on the news, while Binance halted withdrawals and said it would use company funds to cover the losses. Stablecoin issuers including El Salvador-based Tether and the Trump-backed World Liberty Financial froze about half of the stolen assets. The exchange said customer funds were safe and it was working with partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It said earlier on Friday it expected to resume withdrawal services in the next 48 hours. It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion. Binance said it had set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1 billion. “We NEVER use any customer funds, so they are not impacted,” Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said ‌in a post on ‌X. Teng described the breach as a “complex attack” that was not carried out by one person and ​included ‌a ⁠compromised laptop ​as well ⁠as malicious software designed to delete traces and evidence of its activity as it went along, “making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate.” The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, Internet-connected wallet in a way that did not pass through normal approval controls, Teng said. Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million. The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs ⁠and Chainalysis. TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a ‌2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea. “TRM attributes the attack ‌to ... North Korea’s elite hacking unit,” the firm said in an analysis on its website. Both TRM ​and Chainalysis said they were highly confident North Korea was responsible. “This incident ‌is almost certainly the single largest known theft of any kind,” British blockchain analysts Elliptic said. North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for ‌espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well as cybersecurity experts. North Korea routinely denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment. Binance is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the United States Secret Service (USSS), a person familiar with the situation told Reuters. The FBI said it was “aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate ‌investigative steps.” The USSS did not respond to an emailed request for comment. Abu Dhabi’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance’s main operating license, said it was “engaging closely with Binance and monitoring the incident.” “It’s the biggest ⁠hack in history,” Aravind Srinivasan at market ⁠maker GSR said, as crypto prices fell broadly. Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3 percent to a two-month low of $2,178 before markets stabilized.
