North Korean hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance , the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, in a lightning-fast theft that an insider has called “the largest bank heist in human history.” Cybercriminals swiped the digital coins out of Binance wallets within a mere 20 minutes starting at 4:30 p.m. ET Thursday, exploiting the system by hacking into an engineer’s laptop, according to analytics firm TRM Labs and industry insiders. Binance initially said the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop. In an update Friday, Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, said the company’s security team has “uncovered additional points of breach,” suggesting it was a complex attack carried out by more than one person. “The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism … making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate,” Teng said, adding that Binance’s security team is still deep in the throes of the investigation. TraderTraitor, the North Korean hacking group suspected of the crime, is known for pulling off unparalleled lootings by using algorithms to spread the riches across global crypto networks faster than any human could – making them virtually impossible to recover. US officials have said cybercrime attacks fund roughly half of North Korea’s missile program. Binance said Friday it has started to recover some of the stolen assets. About $2.8 billion was quickly frozen by stablecoin providers – but roughly $3 billion is likely gone forever, as it was unable to be frozen, according to analytics firms. The crypto exchange added that it’s on track to allow customers to make withdrawals within two days and that it has set over $6 billion of company funds aside to cover customers’ losses. It suspended withdrawals and vowed to cover all losses immediately after the attack. Meanwhile, co-CEO Changpeng Zhao tried to stop Tesla and SpaceX billionaire Elon Musk from adding to the chaos online, telling him that it’s a “bad time to troll.” Musk posted several laughing- and grimacing-face emojis on X, his social-media platform, reacting to the news. Zhao responded by reminding Musk that Binance holds a stake in his businesses worth more than $1 billion. “Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop,” Zhao wrote. “Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!” Bitcoin dropped below $80,000 for the first time in a month, ether fell to a two-month low of $2,230 and crypto-related stocks plummeted as the hack served as a stunning reminder that the crypto industry still remains a largely unregulated Wild West. “You could probably say it was the biggest hack ever in terms of monetary value,” Nic Puckrin, CEO of Coin Bureau, told The Post. Binance said it is working with law enforcement, including the Secret Service; blockchain intelligence firms; token issuers; and other exchanges to trace and recover the stolen funds, promising to do everything possible to “ensure that these bad actors will be held accountable.” The exchange is also conducting a full security review across the company, including endpoints, cloud and key management, according to Teng. The company said there is no evidence of the hacker still having direct access to funds. TRM Labs, the US-based blockchain intelligence firm that pinned the attack on TraderTraitor, described the cybercriminal group as North Korea’s elite hacking unit. “We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said, noting that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.” Chainalysis co-founder Jonathan Levin also suspected North Korean hackers, writing that they “are up to their old tricks.” A massive $1.5 billion heist targeting crypto exchange Bybit last year was also pinned on the North Korean cybercrime group, given the code name TraderTraitor by the FBI. Last month, North Korean groups were suspected in the theft of over $350 million in crypto in a hack of crypto exchange Bitget. extraction.body: Stablecoin issuers froze about $2.4 billion of the roughly $6.4 billion stolen. The rest exceeds Binance’s insurance fund, and the man promising to make users whole isn’t supposed to be running the company. A notorious North Korean cybercrime group has stolen around $6.4 billion in cryptoassets from multiple hot wallets a belonging to Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, and still controls around $3 billion of it after stablecoin issuers and other protocols froze what they could. These estimates are still in flux as various platforms work to freeze tokens or otherwise thwart the attacker from cashing out, and as both Binance and independent security researchers continue their investigations. Unlike many supposedly “multi-billion dollar” crypto hacks, where the headline figure relies on the notional value of illiquid assets that could never be sold for anywhere near that amount, the majority of these stolen assets were major stablecoins, bitcoin, ethereum, and other fairly liquid tokens. Binance has estimated the total theft at $6.3 billion; external estimates later revised the total up to around $6.4 billion. At least $5.5 billion of these were liquid assets. Tether announced they had frozen at least $1.567 billion of the stolen USDT, and Circle has frozen around $800 million of stolen USDC. World Liberty Financial froze the $27 million in USD1 stolen by the attacker, and the Arbitrum ethereum layer-2 network froze an additional $30.5 million that had moved to its network. The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion . Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who is legally not allowed to have any active role with the company [ I98 ] yet still has remarkable amounts of inside knowledge into its inner workings, posted on Twitter less than an hour after the theft that “User funds are safe!”, adding early estimates of how much Tether and Circle had frozen. He added, “I don't manage Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.” He later tweeted “Loss might be a bit higher than [$1 billion], but will cover.” (Why a person who is barred from any control over Binance would be the one promising this is an exercise I will leave to the reader.) extraction.body: The Binance hack resulted in approximately $6.3 billion in crypto outflows across 10 blockchains. Investigators believe a compromised DevOps laptop and an exploit involving Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality helped attackers drain exchange-controlled wallets. The Binance hack has emerged as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, after attackers moved approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets from wallets belonging to the world's largest crypto exchange. The incident, which occurred on October 29, 2026, involved unauthorized withdrawals across 10 blockchain networks and may have started with a compromised laptop belonging to a Binance DevOps engineer. Binance's preliminary investigation suggests the attacker used the compromised device to access an internal service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. The exchange said it found no evidence that wallet private keys had been leaked. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs traced approximately $6.36 billion in outflows and attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking group. The investigation also revealed that attackers used Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality to gain control over a hot wallet's transaction execution. Binance said it had worked with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion in assets and pledged to cover all losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds. Binance's initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop as the possible entry point for the attack. According to the exchange, the attacker used access from the compromised device to reach an internal service container. This container reportedly provided a route to systems involved in processing withdrawal transactions. Instead of directly stealing wallet private keys, the attackers allegedly exploited the infrastructure responsible for authorizing transactions. This distinction is important. Cryptocurrency exchanges use hot wallets to process withdrawals, and these wallets must interact with internal applications and transaction-signing systems. If an attacker gains control over an application or service authorized to request transactions, they may be able to move funds without extracting the underlying private keys. Binance said its investigation found no evidence of a private-key leak. However, the exchange has not yet published a complete technical post-mortem explaining exactly how the laptop was compromised or how the attacker gained access to the internal signing infrastructure. One of the most significant findings from the blockchain investigation concerns Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality. Introduced through Ethereum's Pectra upgrade, EIP-7702 allows externally owned accounts to temporarily delegate transaction execution to smart-contract code through signed authorizations. TRM Labs reported that the attacker used this mechanism to turn a Binance hot wallet into a sweeper account controlled by the attacker. The process involved 50 pre-signed authorizations prepared in advance. Each authorization corresponded to a different transaction nonce, which determines the sequence of transactions from an Ethereum account. More importantly, the delegation remained active. As additional funds arrived in the Binance hot wallet, the attacker could execute further transfers instead of relying on a single withdrawal. TRM Labs reported that the wallet was swept multiple times. The attacker also used the compromised wallet's execution capabilities to access funds associated with a separate Binance smart account. This method allowed the attackers to exploit transaction authorization rather than directly extracting the wallet's private key. The attack was not limited to Ethereum. TRM Labs traced approximately $6.36 billion in transfers from Binance-attributed wallets across 10 blockchain networks. According to TRM Labs, most of the initial outflows happened within approximately 20 minutes, beginning at 20:05 UTC on October 29. A later wave of transactions involved wallets on Avalanche and Polygon. Ethereum accounted for the largest share of the reported outflows, with approximately $3.79 billion in assets transferred. Bitcoin outflows reached approximately 18,270 BTC, worth around $1.47 billion at the time of the transfers. The attackers also moved substantial quantities of stablecoins, including USDT and USDC, alongside other digital assets. The activity across multiple networks suggests that the incident involved more than an isolated Ethereum wallet exploit. TRM Labs believes the attackers gained access to Binance's broader hot-wallet signing infrastructure, although the exchange has yet to confirm the complete technical explanation. After draining the wallets, the attackers began moving and converting the stolen assets to make recovery more difficult. Binance worked with blockchain intelligence firms, stablecoin issuers, and other industry participants to limit the movement of stolen funds. The exchange initially reported that approximately $3 billion had been frozen on-chain. TRM Labs separately estimated that around $2.7 billion in assets had been frozen through stablecoin issuers and blockchain-level interventions at the time of its analysis. Tether, Circle, Ripple, and World Liberty Financial participated in freezing affected stablecoins. Arbitrum's Security Council also froze assets on its network. Despite these interventions, TRM Labs estimated that the attacker still controlled more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth approximately $2.4 billion at the time of its analysis. Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals across several networks while conducting security checks and coordinating with its partners. The response highlights the importance of emergency reserves in centralized exchange security. TRM Labs attributed the Binance hack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking unit. The firm's assessment was based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence, as well as similarities between this incident and previous attacks associated with the group. Chainalysis also reportedly linked the attack to North Korean hackers. However, Binance has not officially identified the attackers, and the attribution remains an assessment by blockchain intelligence firms rather than a publicly confirmed government finding. TraderTraitor has previously been associated with major cryptocurrency thefts, including the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025. The Binance incident highlights the continued threat posed by sophisticated attackers targeting centralized exchanges and their internal infrastructure. State-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor was formed around 2016 and tasked with stealing cryptocurrency, according to the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, a group of 11 nations including the US that tracks North Korean sanctions violations.
A massive $1.5 billion heist targeting crypto exchange Bybit last year was also pinned on the North Korean cybercrime group, given the code name TraderTraitor by the FBI.
US officials have said cybercrime attacks fund roughly half of North Korea’s missile program.
Musk posted several laughing- and grimacing-face emojis on X, his social-media platform, reacting to the news.
Zhao responded by reminding Musk that Binance holds a stake in his businesses worth more than $1 billion.
Cybercriminals swiped the digital coins out of Binance wallets within a mere 20 minutes starting at 4:30 p.m.

extraction.body: See more of our coverage in your search results. North Korean hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance , the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, in a lightning-fast theft that an insider has called “the largest bank heist in human history.” Cybercriminals swiped the digital coins out of Binance wallets within a mere 20 minutes starting at 4:30 p.m. ET Thursday, exploiting the system by hacking into an engineer’s laptop, according to analytics firm TRM Labs and industry insiders. Binance initially said the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop. In an update Friday, Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, said the company’s security team has “uncovered additional points of breach,” suggesting it was a complex attack carried out by more than one person. “The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism … making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate,” Teng said, adding that Binance’s security team is still deep in the throes of the investigation. TraderTraitor, the North Korean hacking group suspected of the crime, is known for pulling off unparalleled lootings by using algorithms to spread the riches across global crypto networks faster than any human could – making them virtually impossible to recover. US officials have said cybercrime attacks fund roughly half of North Korea’s missile program. Binance said Friday it has started to recover some of the stolen assets. About $2.8 billion was quickly frozen by stablecoin providers – but roughly $3 billion is likely gone forever, as it was unable to be frozen, according to analytics firms. The crypto exchange added that it’s on track to allow customers to make withdrawals within two days and that it has set over $6 billion of company funds aside to cover customers’ losses. It suspended withdrawals and vowed to cover all losses immediately after the attack. Meanwhile, co-CEO Changpeng Zhao tried to stop Tesla and SpaceX billionaire Elon Musk from adding to the chaos online, telling him that it’s a “bad time to troll.” Musk posted several laughing- and grimacing-face emojis on X, his social-media platform, reacting to the news. Zhao responded by reminding Musk that Binance holds a stake in his businesses worth more than $1 billion. “Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop,” Zhao wrote. “Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!” Bitcoin dropped below $80,000 for the first time in a month, ether fell to a two-month low of $2,230 and crypto-related stocks plummeted as the hack served as a stunning reminder that the crypto industry still remains a largely unregulated Wild West. “You could probably say it was the biggest hack ever in terms of monetary value,” Nic Puckrin, CEO of Coin Bureau, told The Post. Binance said it is working with law enforcement, including the Secret Service; blockchain intelligence firms; token issuers; and other exchanges to trace and recover the stolen funds, promising to do everything possible to “ensure that these bad actors will be held accountable.” The exchange is also conducting a full security review across the company, including endpoints, cloud and key management, according to Teng. The company said there is no evidence of the hacker still having direct access to funds. TRM Labs, the US-based blockchain intelligence firm that pinned the attack on TraderTraitor, described the cybercriminal group as North Korea’s elite hacking unit. “We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said, noting that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.” Chainalysis co-founder Jonathan Levin also suspected North Korean hackers, writing that they “are up to their old tricks.” A massive $1.5 billion heist targeting crypto exchange Bybit last year was also pinned on the North Korean cybercrime group, given the code name TraderTraitor by the FBI. Last month, North Korean groups were suspected in the theft of over $350 million in crypto in a hack of crypto exchange Bitget. State-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor was formed around 2016 and tasked with stealing cryptocurrency, according to the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, a group of 11 nations including the US that tracks North Korean sanctions violations. Binance maintains a $1 billion bitcoin reserve asset fund for users designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website.

Binance initially said the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop. In an update Friday, Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, said the company’s security team has “uncovered additional points of breach,” suggesting it was a complex attack carried out by more than one person.

“The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism … making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate,” Teng said, adding that Binance’s security team is still deep in the throes of the investigation.

TraderTraitor, the North Korean hacking group suspected of the crime, is known for pulling off unparalleled lootings by using algorithms to spread the riches across global crypto networks faster than any human could – making them virtually impossible to recover. US officials have said cybercrime attacks fund roughly half of North Korea’s missile program.

Binance said Friday it has started to recover some of the stolen assets. About $2.8 billion was quickly frozen by stablecoin providers – but roughly $3 billion is likely gone forever, as it was unable to be frozen, according to analytics firms.

The crypto exchange added that it’s on track to allow customers to make withdrawals within two days and that it has set over $6 billion of company funds aside to cover customers’ losses. It suspended withdrawals and vowed to cover all losses immediately after the attack.
Meanwhile, co-CEO Changpeng Zhao tried to stop Tesla and SpaceX billionaire Elon Musk from adding to the chaos online, telling him that it’s a “bad time to troll.”

Musk posted several laughing- and grimacing-face emojis on X, his social-media platform, reacting to the news. Zhao responded by reminding Musk that Binance holds a stake in his businesses worth more than $1 billion.

“Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop,” Zhao wrote. “Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!”

Bitcoin dropped below $80,000 for the first time in a month, ether fell to a two-month low of $2,230 and crypto-related stocks plummeted as the hack served as a stunning reminder that the crypto industry still remains a largely unregulated Wild West.
“You could probably say it was the biggest hack ever in terms of monetary value,” Nic Puckrin, CEO of Coin Bureau, told The Post.

Binance said it is working with law enforcement, including the Secret Service; blockchain intelligence firms; token issuers; and other exchanges to trace and recover the stolen funds, promising to do everything possible to “ensure that these bad actors will be held accountable.”
The exchange is also conducting a full security review across the company, including endpoints, cloud and key management, according to Teng.
The company said there is no evidence of the hacker still having direct access to funds.
TRM Labs, the US-based blockchain intelligence firm that pinned the attack on TraderTraitor, described the cybercriminal group as North Korea’s elite hacking unit.
“We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said, noting that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.”
Chainalysis co-founder Jonathan Levin also suspected North Korean hackers, writing that they “are up to their old tricks.”
A massive $1.5 billion heist targeting crypto exchange Bybit last year was also pinned on the North Korean cybercrime group, given the code name TraderTraitor by the FBI.
Last month, North Korean groups were suspected in the theft of over $350 million in crypto in a hack of crypto exchange Bitget.

State-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor was formed around 2016 and tasked with stealing cryptocurrency, according to the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, a group of 11 nations including the US that tracks North Korean sanctions violations.
Binance maintains a $1 billion bitcoin reserve asset fund for users designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website.

World Liberty Financial froze the $27 million in USD1 stolen by the attacker, and the Arbitrum ethereum layer-2 network froze an additional $30.5 million that had moved to its network. The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion . extraction.body: The Binance hack resulted in approximately $6.3 billion in crypto outflows across 10 blockchains. Investigators believe a compromised DevOps laptop and an exploit involving Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality helped attackers drain exchange-controlled wallets. The Binance hack has emerged as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, after attackers moved approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets from wallets belonging to the world's largest crypto exchange. The incident, which occurred on October 29, 2026, involved unauthorized withdrawals across 10 blockchain networks and may have started with a compromised laptop belonging to a Binance DevOps engineer. Binance's preliminary investigation suggests the attacker used the compromised device to access an internal service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. The exchange said it found no evidence that wallet private keys had been leaked. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs traced approximately $6.36 billion in outflows and attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking group. The investigation also revealed that attackers used Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality to gain control over a hot wallet's transaction execution. Binance said it had worked with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion in assets and pledged to cover all losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds. Binance's initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop as the possible entry point for the attack. According to the exchange, the attacker used access from the compromised device to reach an internal service container. This container reportedly provided a route to systems involved in processing withdrawal transactions. Instead of directly stealing wallet private keys, the attackers allegedly exploited the infrastructure responsible for authorizing transactions. This distinction is important. Cryptocurrency exchanges use hot wallets to process withdrawals, and these wallets must interact with internal applications and transaction-signing systems. If an attacker gains control over an application or service authorized to request transactions, they may be able to move funds without extracting the underlying private keys. Binance said its investigation found no evidence of a private-key leak. However, the exchange has not yet published a complete technical post-mortem explaining exactly how the laptop was compromised or how the attacker gained access to the internal signing infrastructure. One of the most significant findings from the blockchain investigation concerns Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality. Introduced through Ethereum's Pectra upgrade, EIP-7702 allows externally owned accounts to temporarily delegate transaction execution to smart-contract code through signed authorizations. TRM Labs reported that the attacker used this mechanism to turn a Binance hot wallet into a sweeper account controlled by the attacker. The process involved 50 pre-signed authorizations prepared in advance. Each authorization corresponded to a different transaction nonce, which determines the sequence of transactions from an Ethereum account. More importantly, the delegation remained active. As additional funds arrived in the Binance hot wallet, the attacker could execute further transfers instead of relying on a single withdrawal. TRM Labs reported that the wallet was swept multiple times. The attacker also used the compromised wallet's execution capabilities to access funds associated with a separate Binance smart account. This method allowed the attackers to exploit transaction authorization rather than directly extracting the wallet's private key. The attack was not limited to Ethereum. TRM Labs traced approximately $6.36 billion in transfers from Binance-attributed wallets across 10 blockchain networks. A later wave of transactions involved wallets on Avalanche and Polygon. Ethereum accounted for the largest share of the reported outflows, with approximately $3.79 billion in assets transferred. The attackers also moved substantial quantities of stablecoins, including USDT and USDC, alongside other digital assets. The activity across multiple networks suggests that the incident involved more than an isolated Ethereum wallet exploit. TRM Labs believes the attackers gained access to Binance's broader hot-wallet signing infrastructure, although the exchange has yet to confirm the complete technical explanation. After draining the wallets, the attackers began moving and converting the stolen assets to make recovery more difficult. Binance worked with blockchain intelligence firms, stablecoin issuers, and other industry participants to limit the movement of stolen funds. The exchange initially reported that approximately $3 billion had been frozen on-chain. The response highlights the importance of emergency reserves in centralized exchange security. The firm's assessment was based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence, as well as similarities between this incident and previous attacks associated with the group. Chainalysis also reportedly linked the attack to North Korean hackers. The rest exceeds Binance’s insurance fund, and the man promising to make users whole isn’t supposed to be running the company. A notorious North Korean cybercrime group has stolen around $6.4 billion in cryptoassets from multiple hot wallets a belonging to Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, and still controls around $3 billion of it after stablecoin issuers and other protocols froze what they could. These estimates are still in flux as various platforms work to freeze tokens or otherwise thwart the attacker from cashing out, and as both Binance and independent security researchers continue their investigations. Unlike many supposedly “multi-billion dollar” crypto hacks, where the headline figure relies on the notional value of illiquid assets that could never be sold for anywhere near that amount, the majority of these stolen assets were major stablecoins, bitcoin, ethereum, and other fairly liquid tokens. Binance has estimated the total theft at $6.3 billion; external estimates later revised the total up to around $6.4 billion. At least $5.5 billion of these were liquid assets. Tether announced they had frozen at least $1.567 billion of the stolen USDT, and Circle has frozen around $800 million of stolen USDC. World Liberty Financial froze the $27 million in USD1 stolen by the attacker, and the Arbitrum ethereum layer-2 network froze an additional $30.5 million that had moved to its network. The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion . Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who is legally not allowed to have any active role with the company [ I98 ] yet still has remarkable amounts of inside knowledge into its inner workings, posted on Twitter less than an hour after the theft that “User funds are safe!”, adding early estimates of how much Tether and Circle had frozen. He added, “I don't manage Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.” He later tweeted “Loss might be a bit higher than [$1 billion], but will cover.” (Why a person who is barred from any control over Binance would be the one promising this is an exercise I will leave to the reader.) Binance keeps an emergency insurance fund in case of exploits or other crypto disasters. Its most recent balance report puts it at around $1.3 billion. 1 Unless more is recovered, Binance will either fail to make users whole or dip into its own balance sheet — potentially to the tune of 10 figures. Blockchain security firm TRM Labs has attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group. 3 The group has been linked to other massive cryptocurrency heists, including a massive $1.5 billion theft from the Bybit cryptocurrency exchange in 2025 [ W3IGG ]. This Binance hack has now surpassed the Bybit hack for the largest cryptocurrency theft. I’ve written more about North Korea’s crypto thefts, how they launder the funds, and what the money pays for in a follow-up. The contagion also threatens to spread beyond Binance. A notorious North Korean cybercrime group has stolen around $6.4 billion in cryptoassets from multiple hot wallets a belonging to Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, and still controls around $3 billion of it after stablecoin issuers and other protocols froze what they could. These estimates are still in flux as various platforms work to freeze tokens or otherwise thwart the attacker from cashing out, and as both Binance and independent security researchers continue their investigations.

Unlike many supposedly “multi-billion dollar” crypto hacks, where the headline figure relies on the notional value of illiquid assets that could never be sold for anywhere near that amount, the majority of these stolen assets were major stablecoins, bitcoin, ethereum, and other fairly liquid tokens.

Binance has estimated the total theft at $6.3 billion; external estimates later revised the total up to around $6.4 billion. At least $5.5 billion of these were liquid assets. Tether announced they had frozen at least $1.567 billion of the stolen USDT, and Circle has frozen around $800 million of stolen USDC. World Liberty Financial froze the $27 million in USD1 stolen by the attacker, and the Arbitrum ethereum layer-2 network froze an additional $30.5 million that had moved to its network. The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion .

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who is legally not allowed to have any active role with the company [ I98 ] yet still has remarkable amounts of inside knowledge into its inner workings, posted on Twitter less than an hour after the theft that “User funds are safe!”, adding early estimates of how much Tether and Circle had frozen. He added, “I don't manage Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.”

He later tweeted “Loss might be a bit higher than [$1 billion], but will cover.” (Why a person who is barred from any control over Binance would be the one promising this is an exercise I will leave to the reader.)

Binance keeps an emergency insurance fund in case of exploits or other crypto disasters. Its most recent balance report puts it at around $1.3 billion. 1 Unless more is recovered, Binance will either fail to make users whole or dip into its own balance sheet — potentially to the tune of 10 figures.

This Binance hack has now surpassed the Bybit hack for the largest cryptocurrency theft. extraction.body: The Binance hack resulted in approximately $6.3 billion in crypto outflows across 10 blockchains. Investigators believe a compromised DevOps laptop and an exploit involving Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality helped attackers drain exchange-controlled wallets. The Binance hack has emerged as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, after attackers moved approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets from wallets belonging to the world's largest crypto exchange. The incident, which occurred on October 29, 2026, involved unauthorized withdrawals across 10 blockchain networks and may have started with a compromised laptop belonging to a Binance DevOps engineer. Binance's preliminary investigation suggests the attacker used the compromised device to access an internal service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. The exchange said it found no evidence that wallet private keys had been leaked. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs traced approximately $6.36 billion in outflows and attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking group. The investigation also revealed that attackers used Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality to gain control over a hot wallet's transaction execution. Binance said it had worked with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion in assets and pledged to cover all losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds. Binance's initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop as the possible entry point for the attack. According to the exchange, the attacker used access from the compromised device to reach an internal service container. This container reportedly provided a route to systems involved in processing withdrawal transactions. Instead of directly stealing wallet private keys, the attackers allegedly exploited the infrastructure responsible for authorizing transactions. This distinction is important. Cryptocurrency exchanges use hot wallets to process withdrawals, and these wallets must interact with internal applications and transaction-signing systems. If an attacker gains control over an application or service authorized to request transactions, they may be able to move funds without extracting the underlying private keys. Binance said its investigation found no evidence of a private-key leak. However, the exchange has not yet published a complete technical post-mortem explaining exactly how the laptop was compromised or how the attacker gained access to the internal signing infrastructure. One of the most significant findings from the blockchain investigation concerns Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality. Introduced through Ethereum's Pectra upgrade, EIP-7702 allows externally owned accounts to temporarily delegate transaction execution to smart-contract code through signed authorizations. TRM Labs reported that the attacker used this mechanism to turn a Binance hot wallet into a sweeper account controlled by the attacker. The process involved 50 pre-signed authorizations prepared in advance. Each authorization corresponded to a different transaction nonce, which determines the sequence of transactions from an Ethereum account. More importantly, the delegation remained active. As additional funds arrived in the Binance hot wallet, the attacker could execute further transfers instead of relying on a single withdrawal. TRM Labs reported that the wallet was swept multiple times. The attacker also used the compromised wallet's execution capabilities to access funds associated with a separate Binance smart account. This method allowed the attackers to exploit transaction authorization rather than directly extracting the wallet's private key. The attack was not limited to Ethereum. TRM Labs traced approximately $6.36 billion in transfers from Binance-attributed wallets across 10 blockchain networks. According to TRM Labs, most of the initial outflows happened within approximately 20 minutes, beginning at 20:05 UTC on October 29. A later wave of transactions involved wallets on Avalanche and Polygon. Ethereum accounted for the largest share of the reported outflows, with approximately $3.79 billion in assets transferred. Bitcoin outflows reached approximately 18,270 BTC, worth around $1.47 billion at the time of the transfers. The attackers also moved substantial quantities of stablecoins, including USDT and USDC, alongside other digital assets. The activity across multiple networks suggests that the incident involved more than an isolated Ethereum wallet exploit. TRM Labs believes the attackers gained access to Binance's broader hot-wallet signing infrastructure, although the exchange has yet to confirm the complete technical explanation. After draining the wallets, the attackers began moving and converting the stolen assets to make recovery more difficult. Binance worked with blockchain intelligence firms, stablecoin issuers, and other industry participants to limit the movement of stolen funds. The exchange initially reported that approximately $3 billion had been frozen on-chain. TRM Labs separately estimated that around $2.7 billion in assets had been frozen through stablecoin issuers and blockchain-level interventions at the time of its analysis. Tether, Circle, Ripple, and World Liberty Financial participated in freezing affected stablecoins. Arbitrum's Security Council also froze assets on its network. Despite these interventions, TRM Labs estimated that the attacker still controlled more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth approximately $2.4 billion at the time of its analysis. Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals across several networks while conducting security checks and coordinating with its partners. The response highlights the importance of emergency reserves in centralized exchange security. TRM Labs attributed the Binance hack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking unit. The firm's assessment was based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence, as well as similarities between this incident and previous attacks associated with the group. Chainalysis also reportedly linked the attack to North Korean hackers. However, Binance has not officially identified the attackers, and the attribution remains an assessment by blockchain intelligence firms rather than a publicly confirmed government finding. TraderTraitor has previously been associated with major cryptocurrency thefts, including the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025. The Binance incident highlights the continued threat posed by sophisticated attackers targeting centralized exchanges and their internal infrastructure. North Korean hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance , the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, in a lightning-fast theft that an insider has called “the largest bank heist in human history.” Cybercriminals swiped the digital coins out of Binance wallets within a mere 20 minutes starting at 4:30 p.m. ET Thursday, exploiting the system by hacking into an engineer’s laptop, according to analytics firm TRM Labs and industry insiders. Binance initially said the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop. In an update Friday, Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, said the company’s security team has “uncovered additional points of breach,” suggesting it was a complex attack carried out by more than one person. “The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism … making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate,” Teng said, adding that Binance’s security team is still deep in the throes of the investigation. TraderTraitor, the North Korean hacking group suspected of the crime, is known for pulling off unparalleled lootings by using algorithms to spread the riches across global crypto networks faster than any human could – making them virtually impossible to recover. US officials have said cybercrime attacks fund roughly half of North Korea’s missile program. Binance said Friday it has started to recover some of the stolen assets. About $2.8 billion was quickly frozen by stablecoin providers – but roughly $3 billion is likely gone forever, as it was unable to be frozen, according to analytics firms. The crypto exchange added that it’s on track to allow customers to make withdrawals within two days and that it has set over $6 billion of company funds aside to cover customers’ losses. It suspended withdrawals and vowed to cover all losses immediately after the attack. Meanwhile, co-CEO Changpeng Zhao tried to stop Tesla and SpaceX billionaire Elon Musk from adding to the chaos online, telling him that it’s a “bad time to troll.” Musk posted several laughing- and grimacing-face emojis on X, his social-media platform, reacting to the news. Zhao responded by reminding Musk that Binance holds a stake in his businesses worth more than $1 billion. “Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop,” Zhao wrote. “Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!” Bitcoin dropped below $80,000 for the first time in a month, ether fell to a two-month low of $2,230 and crypto-related stocks plummeted as the hack served as a stunning reminder that the crypto industry still remains a largely unregulated Wild West. “You could probably say it was the biggest hack ever in terms of monetary value,” Nic Puckrin, CEO of Coin Bureau, told The Post. Binance said it is working with law enforcement, including the Secret Service; blockchain intelligence firms; token issuers; and other exchanges to trace and recover the stolen funds, promising to do everything possible to “ensure that these bad actors will be held accountable.” The exchange is also conducting a full security review across the company, including endpoints, cloud and key management, according to Teng. The company said there is no evidence of the hacker still having direct access to funds. TRM Labs, the US-based blockchain intelligence firm that pinned the attack on TraderTraitor, described the cybercriminal group as North Korea’s elite hacking unit. “We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said, noting that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.” Chainalysis co-founder Jonathan Levin also suspected North Korean hackers, writing that they “are up to their old tricks.” A massive $1.5 billion heist targeting crypto exchange Bybit last year was also pinned on the North Korean cybercrime group, given the code name TraderTraitor by the FBI. Last month, North Korean groups were suspected in the theft of over $350 million in crypto in a hack of crypto exchange Bitget. Binance maintains a $1 billion bitcoin reserve asset fund for users designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website.

Meanwhile, co-CEO Changpeng Zhao tried to stop Tesla and SpaceX billionaire Elon Musk from adding to the chaos online, telling him that it’s a “bad time to troll.”

Musk posted several laughing- and grimacing-face emojis on X, his social-media platform, reacting to the news. Zhao responded by reminding Musk that Binance holds a stake in his businesses worth more than $1 billion.

“Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop,” Zhao wrote. “Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!”

Bitcoin dropped below $80,000 for the first time in a month, ether fell to a two-month low of $2,230 and crypto-related stocks plummeted as the hack served as a stunning reminder that the crypto industry still remains a largely unregulated Wild West.
“You could probably say it was the biggest hack ever in terms of monetary value,” Nic Puckrin, CEO of Coin Bureau, told The Post.

Binance said it is working with law enforcement, including the Secret Service; blockchain intelligence firms; token issuers; and other exchanges to trace and recover the stolen funds, promising to do everything possible to “ensure that these bad actors will be held accountable.”
The exchange is also conducting a full security review across the company, including endpoints, cloud and key management, according to Teng.
The company said there is no evidence of the hacker still having direct access to funds.
TRM Labs, the US-based blockchain intelligence firm that pinned the attack on TraderTraitor, described the cybercriminal group as North Korea’s elite hacking unit.
“We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said, noting that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.”
Chainalysis co-founder Jonathan Levin also suspected North Korean hackers, writing that they “are up to their old tricks.”
A massive $1.5 billion heist targeting crypto exchange Bybit last year was also pinned on the North Korean cybercrime group, given the code name TraderTraitor by the FBI.
Last month, North Korean groups were suspected in the theft of over $350 million in crypto in a hack of crypto exchange Bitget.

State-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor was formed around 2016 and tasked with stealing cryptocurrency, according to the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, a group of 11 nations including the US that tracks North Korean sanctions violations.
Binance maintains a $1 billion bitcoin reserve asset fund for users designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website.

World Liberty Financial froze the $27 million in USD1 stolen by the attacker, and the Arbitrum ethereum layer-2 network froze an additional $30.5 million that had moved to its network. The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion . He added, “I don't manage Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.” He later tweeted “Loss might be a bit higher than [$1 billion], but will cover.” (Why a person who is barred from any control over Binance would be the one promising this is an exercise I will leave to the reader.) extraction.body: The Binance hack resulted in approximately $6.3 billion in crypto outflows across 10 blockchains. Investigators believe a compromised DevOps laptop and an exploit involving Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality helped attackers drain exchange-controlled wallets. The Binance hack has emerged as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, after attackers moved approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets from wallets belonging to the world's largest crypto exchange. The incident, which occurred on October 29, 2026, involved unauthorized withdrawals across 10 blockchain networks and may have started with a compromised laptop belonging to a Binance DevOps engineer. Binance's preliminary investigation suggests the attacker used the compromised device to access an internal service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. The exchange said it found no evidence that wallet private keys had been leaked. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs traced approximately $6.36 billion in outflows and attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking group. The investigation also revealed that attackers used Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality to gain control over a hot wallet's transaction execution. Binance said it had worked with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion in assets and pledged to cover all losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds. Binance's initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop as the possible entry point for the attack. According to the exchange, the attacker used access from the compromised device to reach an internal service container. This container reportedly provided a route to systems involved in processing withdrawal transactions. Instead of directly stealing wallet private keys, the attackers allegedly exploited the infrastructure responsible for authorizing transactions. This distinction is important. Cryptocurrency exchanges use hot wallets to process withdrawals, and these wallets must interact with internal applications and transaction-signing systems. If an attacker gains control over an application or service authorized to request transactions, they may be able to move funds without extracting the underlying private keys. Binance said its investigation found no evidence of a private-key leak. However, the exchange has not yet published a complete technical post-mortem explaining exactly how the laptop was compromised or how the attacker gained access to the internal signing infrastructure. One of the most significant findings from the blockchain investigation concerns Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality. Introduced through Ethereum's Pectra upgrade, EIP-7702 allows externally owned accounts to temporarily delegate transaction execution to smart-contract code through signed authorizations. TRM Labs reported that the attacker used this mechanism to turn a Binance hot wallet into a sweeper account controlled by the attacker. The process involved 50 pre-signed authorizations prepared in advance. Each authorization corresponded to a different transaction nonce, which determines the sequence of transactions from an Ethereum account. More importantly, the delegation remained active. As additional funds arrived in the Binance hot wallet, the attacker could execute further transfers instead of relying on a single withdrawal. TRM Labs reported that the wallet was swept multiple times. The attacker also used the compromised wallet's execution capabilities to access funds associated with a separate Binance smart account. This method allowed the attackers to exploit transaction authorization rather than directly extracting the wallet's private key. The attack was not limited to Ethereum. TRM Labs traced approximately $6.36 billion in transfers from Binance-attributed wallets across 10 blockchain networks. According to TRM Labs, most of the initial outflows happened within approximately 20 minutes, beginning at 20:05 UTC on October 29. extraction.body: On October 29, 2026, Binance , the world’s largest crypto exchange by trading volume, was hit by a security breach. The exchange estimates the total impact at around $6.3 billion . If the figures hold, it would be the largest crypto theft on record, more than four times the roughly $1.46 billion taken from Bybit in February 2025. This article covers what is known so far about how the attack happened, how much was affected, who may be behind it, and what users should keep in mind. According to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic , attackers made unauthorized withdrawals from Binance “hot wallets” (wallets kept online for day-to-day withdrawals) on 11 blockchains. Elliptic says the first transfer was around 20:05 UTC, when 233 million XRP left Binance wallets. Within about 30 minutes, wallets on Ethereum, Bitcoin, Solana, Tron, Base and several other networks had also been drained. A second wave followed after 23:00 UTC. Elliptic puts the total at $6.43 billion. Arkham estimates $6.01 billion across nine blockchains. Binance’s own figure of about $6.3 billion is an estimate of the total impact, not a confirmed final loss. The exchange has said the numbers may change as the investigation continues. Binance’s initial investigation suggests that the attack “may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop.” A DevOps engineer helps run the company’s technical systems. Binance says the compromised laptop let the attacker reach a “service container,” an isolated piece of software inside its systems, and submit withdrawal transactions without authorization. The exchange said it found no evidence that any wallet’s private key had leaked. In a later update, Binance said it had “uncovered additional points of breach” and described the incident as “ a complex attack “. Co-CEO Richard Teng said it “was not a single ‘one-click’ action.” Elliptic’s on-chain analysis suggests the attacker got Binance’s own systems to approve transactions, rather than stealing its keys. The exact method has not been confirmed. Binance has promised a detailed technical post-mortem once its investigation is finished. Stablecoins, tokens pegged to the US dollar, made up a large share of the affected assets. Their issuers can freeze them, and that limited part of the damage. According to Elliptic: Binance says about $3 billion has been frozen on-chain so far. Elliptic has independently confirmed $2.84 billion. Bitcoin, XRP, Solana and other native coins have no central issuer, so no one can freeze them. Elliptic estimates the attacker still controls around $3.3 billion in assets that cannot be frozen. TRM Labs said it has “high confidence” that TraderTraitor carried out the attack. TraderTraitor is a North Korea-linked hacking group associated with the Lazarus Group. Elliptic has also attributed the theft to North Korea. It pointed to a shared laundering address linked to the September 2026 Bitget exploit and to attack methods similar to the Bybit hack. Elliptic also noted reasons for caution, including that the overlap in funds is small. No government agency has confirmed who was responsible, and Binance says its investigation “has not attributed responsibility to any individual.” Binance paused deposits and withdrawals, revoked the authorization for the affected addresses, and began working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms. The exchange says it will cover all losses from its SAFU fund (an emergency reserve for users) and company funds, and states that “user funds are safe.” Deposits are now working normally. As of Friday morning, Binance said it was on track to restore withdrawals within 45 hours. It also plans to publish an updated Proof of Reserves, a report showing it holds enough assets to cover customer balances, once the repair work is complete. This breach does not appear to have involved broken cryptography. According to early findings, it targeted the people and internal systems around the wallets. Elliptic noted a similar pattern in the Bybit hack. That shows how much a centralized exchange’s safety depends on its access controls, how it separates internal permissions, and how strictly it follows its security procedures. When you leave crypto on a centralized exchange, the exchange holds it for you. This is called custody. Your access then depends on that company’s security and its decisions, such as pausing withdrawals. Non-custodial services work differently: you keep your coins in your own wallet and control the private keys. That shifts the responsibility for security to you. Major hacks are often followed by scams. Rely only on Binance’s official channels for updates. Be wary of fake support accounts, phishing links, and anyone offering to “recover” funds, because legitimate support will never ask for your seed phrase or private keys. Don’t forget to do your own research before buying any crypto. The views and opinions expressed in this article are solely those of the author. extraction.body: The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, is facing a security incident estimated to have caused $6.3 billion in losses, the highest ever recorded in the history of the digital asset industry. According to information published on October 30, Binance said it had coordinated with partners to freeze the affected assets, of which about $3 billion had been located. The exchange has not updated the status of the remaining $3.3 billion. Binance co-founder Yi He insisted the company will compensate for "all losses caused by the attack." The statement comes as investors question the safety of customer funds held at centralized exchanges and as many are forced to revisit their risk appetite for holding crypto assets. Before the Binance incident was confirmed, the attack on the Bybit exchange in February 2025 was still regarded as the largest crypto theft ever officially disclosed, with losses of about $1.5 billion. At the time, hackers took control of a transaction involving Bybit's Ethereum cold wallet and moved a large amount of assets to unauthorized addresses. Notably, the attackers did not break the security mechanism of the Ethereum blockchain but instead exploited the transaction approval system of a third-party wallet provider: the transaction confirmation interface was tampered with so that staff saw an ordinary transfer order, while the actual content was re-signed to change control of the wallet. On February 26, 2025, the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) attributed the incident to a North Korea-linked cyber actor group called TraderTraitor; the stolen funds were subsequently converted into Bitcoin and dispersed across thousands of wallets on multiple blockchain networks. The table below summarizes the largest crypto thefts based on disclosed data: Note: Loss values are calculated at the time of the incident or the time of disclosure; the Binance figure is a preliminary estimate and may change as the investigation expands. Beyond Bybit, the industry's history records many other large-scale incidents. In March 2022, Ronin Network, the blockchain network serving the game Axie Infinity, had 173,600 ETH and 25.5 million USDC stolen, estimated at about $540 million at the time of the attack and rising to more than $600 million when the incident was disclosed due to Ethereum price volatility. The attackers obtained the private keys of 5 of the 9 validation nodes, just enough to meet the threshold needed to approve transactions. The incident occurred on March 23 but was not discovered until March 29, 2022, after a user was unable to execute a withdrawal. U.S. authorities later linked the incident to North Korea's Lazarus hacker group. Before Ronin, in August 2021, Poly Network recorded a smart contract vulnerability that led to about $610 million in assets being moved. What followed was unusual when the perpetrator began returning the money, and by the end of August 2021 the platform announced it had regained control of nearly all the stolen assets, except for a portion of stablecoins that had been frozen. The Binance ecosystem itself had seen several incidents before 2026. In May 2019, the exchange had about 7,000 Bitcoin, equivalent to $41 million at the time, stolen through online phishing and malware; Binance later used its user protection fund to cover the losses. In October 2022, BSC Token Hub, a bridge belonging to BNB Chain, was exploited through a vulnerability to create about 2 million BNB worth more than $550 million; thanks to a network pause and coordinated freezing, most of the funds remained within control, while about $100-130 million was moved to other blockchains. This incident involved bridge infrastructure rather than a direct breach of the Binance exchange. A controversial case is LuBian. In August 2025, blockchain analytics firm Arkham Intelligence published the results of an investigation into the loss of about 127,426 Bitcoin, estimated to be worth $3.5 billion at the time, from wallets linked to this Bitcoin mining group in December 2020. LuBian was said to have carried out more than 1,500 transactions with messages offering to return the Bitcoin, spending about 1.4 BTC just to send the messages. Analysts suspect the vulnerability lay in the private key generation algorithm. The case became more complicated when, in October 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice announced the seizure of about 127,271 Bitcoin, then worth nearly $15 billion, related to the criminal case against Chen Zhi, founder of Prince Group, giving rise to disputes over the origin and ownership of the assets. In Japan, the 2018 Coincheck case was a major milestone when hackers stole NEM worth about $530 million from the exchange's hot wallet. Earlier, the collapse of Mt. Gox in 2014 - an exchange that once handled most global Bitcoin transactions - with losses of about 850,000 Bitcoin, nearly $500 million at the time, forced the exchange to file for bankruptcy and affected tens of thousands of customers. The wave of attacks continued in 2026. In September, the Bitget exchange announced the theft of assets worth about $350 million, a figure later revised to about $387.5 million, showing that initially disclosed losses can change significantly as investigations expand. According to TRM Labs data, in 2025 alone, hackers stole about $2.9 billion in crypto assets through nearly 150 attacks, spanning centralized exchanges, custodial wallets, authentication systems and blockchain bridges. Binance's $6.3 billion scale - if fully confirmed - would far exceed any previous incident, including the $3.5 billion loss at LuBian. passages: The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, is facing a security incident estimated to have caused $6.3 billion in losses, the highest ever recorded in the history of the digital asset industry. According to information published on October 30, Binance said it had coordinated with partners to freeze the affected assets, of which about $3 billion had been located. The exchange has not updated the status of the remaining $3.3 billion.

Binance co-founder Yi He insisted the company will compensate for "all losses caused by the attack." The statement comes as investors question the safety of customer funds held at centralized exchanges and as many are forced to revisit their risk appetite for holding crypto assets.

Before the Binance incident was confirmed, the attack on the Bybit exchange in February 2025 was still regarded as the largest crypto theft ever officially disclosed, with losses of about $1.5 billion. At the time, hackers took control of a transaction involving Bybit's Ethereum cold wallet and moved a large amount of assets to unauthorized addresses. Notably, the attackers did not break the security mechanism of the Ethereum blockchain but instead exploited the transaction approval system of a third-party wallet provider: the transaction confirmation interface was tampered with so that staff saw an ordinary transfer order, while the actual content was re-signed to change control of the wallet. On February 26, 2025, the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) attributed the incident to a North Korea-linked cyber actor group called TraderTraitor; the stolen funds were subsequently converted into Bitcoin and dispersed across thousands of wallets on multiple blockchain networks.
The table below summarizes the largest crypto thefts based on disclosed data:
Note: Loss values are calculated at the time of the incident or the time of disclosure; the Binance figure is a preliminary estimate and may change as the investigation expands.

Beyond Bybit, the industry's history records many other large-scale incidents. In March 2022, Ronin Network, the blockchain network serving the game Axie Infinity, had 173,600 ETH and 25.5 million USDC stolen, estimated at about $540 million at the time of the attack and rising to more than $600 million when the incident was disclosed due to Ethereum price volatility. The attackers obtained the private keys of 5 of the 9 validation nodes, just enough to meet the threshold needed to approve transactions. The incident occurred on March 23 but was not discovered until March 29, 2022, after a user was unable to execute a withdrawal. U.S. authorities later linked the incident to North Korea's Lazarus hacker group.

Before Ronin, in August 2021, Poly Network recorded a smart contract vulnerability that led to about $610 million in assets being moved. What followed was unusual when the perpetrator began returning the money, and by the end of August 2021 the platform announced it had regained control of nearly all the stolen assets, except for a portion of stablecoins that had been frozen.

The Binance ecosystem itself had seen several incidents before 2026. In May 2019, the exchange had about 7,000 Bitcoin, equivalent to $41 million at the time, stolen through online phishing and malware; Binance later used its user protection fund to cover the losses. In October 2022, BSC Token Hub, a bridge belonging to BNB Chain, was exploited through a vulnerability to create about 2 million BNB worth more than $550 million; thanks to a network pause and coordinated freezing, most of the funds remained within control, while about $100-130 million was moved to other blockchains. This incident involved bridge infrastructure rather than a direct breach of the Binance exchange.

A controversial case is LuBian. In August 2025, blockchain analytics firm Arkham Intelligence published the results of an investigation into the loss of about 127,426 Bitcoin, estimated to be worth $3.5 billion at the time, from wallets linked to this Bitcoin mining group in December 2020. LuBian was said to have carried out more than 1,500 transactions with messages offering to return the Bitcoin, spending about 1.4 BTC just to send the messages. Analysts suspect the vulnerability lay in the private key generation algorithm. The case became more complicated when, in October 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice announced the seizure of about 127,271 Bitcoin, then worth nearly $15 billion, related to the criminal case against Chen Zhi, founder of Prince Group, giving rise to disputes over the origin and ownership of the assets.

In Japan, the 2018 Coincheck case was a major milestone when hackers stole NEM worth about $530 million from the exchange's hot wallet. Earlier, the collapse of Mt. Gox in 2014 - an exchange that once handled most global Bitcoin transactions - with losses of about 850,000 Bitcoin, nearly $500 million at the time, forced the exchange to file for bankruptcy and affected tens of thousands of customers.

The wave of attacks continued in 2026. In September, the Bitget exchange announced the theft of assets worth about $350 million, a figure later revised to about $387.5 million, showing that initially disclosed losses can change significantly as investigations expand. According to TRM Labs data, in 2025 alone, hackers stole about $2.9 billion in crypto assets through nearly 150 attacks, spanning centralized exchanges, custodial wallets, authentication systems and blockchain bridges.

passages: Binance, the world’s leading cryptocurrency exchange, has been targeted in what is now considered the largest cyber heist in crypto history, with hackers managing to siphon off approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets.
The breach was disclosed on Thursday and has prompted a swift response from Binance to contain the fallout.
This incident surpasses the previous record set by the Bybit exchange hack in 2025, which involved $1.5 billion and was also linked to North Korean hackers.
Pakistan’s growing crypto community frequently uses Binance for both domestic and international trading, making this breach especially concerning for local users.
However, Binance’s assurance to reimburse losses should provide some relief to Pakistani traders affected by the hack.
Digital asset issuers Tether and Circle froze $1.6 billion in USDT and $800 million in USDC respectively, linked to the theft.
Binance has confirmed that it has frozen roughly half of the stolen assets with assistance from other platforms and vowed to compensate all affected customers fully.
Importantly, this breach only affects Binance.com, the international platform, while Binance.US and Coinbase have reported no involvement or impact from the attack.
Cybersecurity firm TRM Labs identified the hacking group responsible as TraderTraitor, a North Korean-affiliated entity tied to previous major crypto attacks.
As the case unfolds, it highlights the vulnerabilities even the largest crypto platforms face and stresses the need for stronger security measures industry-wide.

extraction.body: Binance, the world’s leading cryptocurrency exchange, has been targeted in what is now considered the largest cyber heist in crypto history, with hackers managing to siphon off approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets. The breach was disclosed on Thursday and has prompted a swift response from Binance to contain the fallout. Initial investigations indicate that the breach started when an engineer’s compromised laptop was exploited, enabling the attacker to extract funds without authorization. This incident surpasses the previous record set by the Bybit exchange hack in 2025, which involved $1.5 billion and was also linked to North Korean hackers. Binance has confirmed that it has frozen roughly half of the stolen assets with assistance from other platforms and vowed to compensate all affected customers fully. To prevent further losses, the exchange has temporarily suspended withdrawals until it assures platform security. Importantly, this breach only affects Binance.com, the international platform, while Binance.US and Coinbase have reported no involvement or impact from the attack. Cybersecurity firm TRM Labs identified the hacking group responsible as TraderTraitor, a North Korean-affiliated entity tied to previous major crypto attacks. TRM expert Ari Redbord described the incident as a significant milestone in the crypto security landscape, warning that the threat remains due to the substantial amount of stolen cryptocurrency that has yet to be recovered. Several industry stakeholders have taken immediate steps to limit the damage. Digital asset issuers Tether and Circle froze $1.6 billion in USDT and $800 million in USDC respectively, linked to the theft. Additionally, World Liberty Financial, associated with US political figures, assisted in freezing stolen funds. The hack led to sharp declines in major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana, reflecting a shaken investor confidence. Pakistan’s growing crypto community frequently uses Binance for both domestic and international trading, making this breach especially concerning for local users. However, Binance’s assurance to reimburse losses should provide some relief to Pakistani traders affected by the hack. Moreover, recent regulatory advancements such as the inclusion of the Pakistan Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (PVARA) under the national Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA) are set to enhance oversight and compliance for crypto exchanges operating within Pakistan, adding a protective layer for users against such cyber threats in the future. As the case unfolds, it highlights the vulnerabilities even the largest crypto platforms face and stresses the need for stronger security measures industry-wide. The impact on global and Pakistani markets serves as a cautionary tale for users and regulators alike amid the rapid expansion of digital asset trading.

extraction.body: On October 29, 2026, Binance , the world’s largest crypto exchange by trading volume, was hit by a security breach. The exchange estimates the total impact at around $6.3 billion . If the figures hold, it would be the largest crypto theft on record, more than four times the roughly $1.46 billion taken from Bybit in February 2025. This article covers what is known so far about how the attack happened, how much was affected, who may be behind it, and what users should keep in mind. According to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic , attackers made unauthorized withdrawals from Binance “hot wallets” (wallets kept online for day-to-day withdrawals) on 11 blockchains. Elliptic says the first transfer was around 20:05 UTC, when 233 million XRP left Binance wallets. Within about 30 minutes, wallets on Ethereum, Bitcoin, Solana, Tron, Base and several other networks had also been drained. A second wave followed after 23:00 UTC. Elliptic puts the total at $6.43 billion. Arkham estimates $6.01 billion across nine blockchains. Binance’s own figure of about $6.3 billion is an estimate of the total impact, not a confirmed final loss. The exchange has said the numbers may change as the investigation continues. Binance’s initial investigation suggests that the attack “may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop.” A DevOps engineer helps run the company’s technical systems. Binance says the compromised laptop let the attacker reach a “service container,” an isolated piece of software inside its systems, and submit withdrawal transactions without authorization. The exchange said it found no evidence that any wallet’s private key had leaked. In a later update, Binance said it had “uncovered additional points of breach” and described the incident as “ a complex attack “. Co-CEO Richard Teng said it “was not a single ‘one-click’ action.” Elliptic’s on-chain analysis suggests the attacker got Binance’s own systems to approve transactions, rather than stealing its keys. The exact method has not been confirmed. Binance has promised a detailed technical post-mortem once its investigation is finished. Stablecoins, tokens pegged to the US dollar, made up a large share of the affected assets. Their issuers can freeze them, and that limited part of the damage. According to Elliptic: Binance says about $3 billion has been frozen on-chain so far. Elliptic has independently confirmed $2.84 billion. Bitcoin, XRP, Solana and other native coins have no central issuer, so no one can freeze them. Elliptic estimates the attacker still controls around $3.3 billion in assets that cannot be frozen. TRM Labs said it has “high confidence” that TraderTraitor carried out the attack. TraderTraitor is a North Korea-linked hacking group associated with the Lazarus Group. Elliptic has also attributed the theft to North Korea. It pointed to a shared laundering address linked to the September 2026 Bitget exploit and to attack methods similar to the Bybit hack. Elliptic also noted reasons for caution, including that the overlap in funds is small. No government agency has confirmed who was responsible, and Binance says its investigation “has not attributed responsibility to any individual.” Binance paused deposits and withdrawals, revoked the authorization for the affected addresses, and began working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms. The exchange says it will cover all losses from its SAFU fund (an emergency reserve for users) and company funds, and states that “user funds are safe.” Deposits are now working normally. As of Friday morning, Binance said it was on track to restore withdrawals within 45 hours. It also plans to publish an updated Proof of Reserves, a report showing it holds enough assets to cover customer balances, once the repair work is complete. This breach does not appear to have involved broken cryptography. According to early findings, it targeted the people and internal systems around the wallets. Elliptic noted a similar pattern in the Bybit hack. That shows how much a centralized exchange’s safety depends on its access controls, how it separates internal permissions, and how strictly it follows its security procedures. When you leave crypto on a centralized exchange, the exchange holds it for you. This is called custody. Your access then depends on that company’s security and its decisions, such as pausing withdrawals. Non-custodial services work differently: you keep your coins in your own wallet and control the private keys. That shifts the responsibility for security to you. Major hacks are often followed by scams. Rely only on Binance’s official channels for updates. Be wary of fake support accounts, phishing links, and anyone offering to “recover” funds, because legitimate support will never ask for your seed phrase or private keys. Don’t forget to do your own research before buying any crypto. The views and opinions expressed in this article are solely those of the author. sources.title: Binance Suffers $6.3 Billion Hack, Crypto’s Largest Breach - NewzTodays
passages: Binance, the world’s leading cryptocurrency exchange, has been targeted in what is now considered the largest cyber heist in crypto history, with hackers managing to siphon off approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets.
The breach was disclosed on Thursday and has prompted a swift response from Binance to contain the fallout.
This incident surpasses the previous record set by the Bybit exchange hack in 2025, which involved $1.5 billion and was also linked to North Korean hackers.
Pakistan’s growing crypto community frequently uses Binance for both domestic and international trading, making this breach especially concerning for local users.
However, Binance’s assurance to reimburse losses should provide some relief to Pakistani traders affected by the hack.
Digital asset issuers Tether and Circle froze $1.6 billion in USDT and $800 million in USDC respectively, linked to the theft.
Binance has confirmed that it has frozen roughly half of the stolen assets with assistance from other platforms and vowed to compensate all affected customers fully.
Importantly, this breach only affects Binance.com, the international platform, while Binance.US and Coinbase have reported no involvement or impact from the attack.
Cybersecurity firm TRM Labs identified the hacking group responsible as TraderTraitor, a North Korean-affiliated entity tied to previous major crypto attacks.
As the case unfolds, it highlights the vulnerabilities even the largest crypto platforms face and stresses the need for stronger security measures industry-wide.
